An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made. This calculation was part of a larger study to determine the $B^0_s$ meson's lifetime and branching fraction for decaying into $K^+K^-$, using approximately 37 inverse picobarns of proton-proton collision data collected at 5.44 TeV center-of-mass energy by the LHCb detector. The results showed a $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time of $0.458\pm0.020(\text{stat})\pm0.007(\text{syst})$ picoseconds. The measured lifetime was then combined with a different estimate of the branching fraction, yielding a total of $9.2\pm0.8(\text{stat})\pm0.3(\text{syst})$ picoseconds.

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a distributed control problem for a stochastic evolution equation. Specifically, it examines the discretized solution of a boundary control problem with an external random disturbance acting on one of the equation's boundaries. The goal of the control is to minimize the impact of this disturbance on the solution of the equation at the other boundary. The numerical solution is obtained using a finite element method, and the resulting scheme is analyzed to ensure it is stable and convergent. To achieve this, the paper employs a semi-discrete and fully discrete stability analysis, with the underlying stochastic equation being formulated as a stochastic evolution equation with a dissipative trait. The paper also considers the convergent scheme for a specific example where the stochastic equation involves a parabolic part.

Our comprehensive investigation of the Pierre Auger Observatory's extensive dataset has enabled us to conduct a precise study of the directional patterns of cosmic rays at extremely high energies. By correlating the arrival directions of the most energetic cosmic rays with various astronomical objects, including active galactic nuclei, blazars, and nearby galaxies, we utilized a sophisticated matching technique to account for false associations. Our findings reveal that the most energetic cosmic rays exhibit a preference for pointing towards blazars that are oriented towards the Galactic Center, specifically those with high polarization properties, and AGN with the same polarization properties oriented towards the celestial equator. We also observed a concentration of cosmic rays associated with nearby galaxies within 5 megaparsecs, particularly those with the characteristics of starburst galaxies. Our research further revealed large-scale cosmic-ray anisotropy patterns in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres, which exhibit distinct shapes and exhibit a 72-month periodicity that coincides with the Earth's rotation around the Sun. We found that the cosmic-ray anisotropy patterns in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres are out of phase with each other by approximately pi, and our simulations suggest that this phenomenon could be attributed to a source of radiation located in the Solar System.
This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a field char zero is solvable, building on a previous discovery that these algebras possess a nilpotent characteristic.

Our research delves into the analysis of fluid flow in high-energy nucleus-nucleus collisions by examining quasi-elastic charged particles within the ALICE experiment at the LHC for Pb-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV. Fluctuations in the $x$-direction were studied using four-particle cumulants to ensure reliability. Results indicate that flow angle fluctuations are correlated with the collision centrality, while flow magnitude fluctuations exhibit a similar dependence on centrality but with a stronger reaction to most peripheral collisions. These findings are consistent with the MMD model and represent the first observation of flow angle fluctuations in nucleus-nucleus collisions.

Maintaining consistency in databases over time is a pressing issue due to the growing frequency of updates and new information being integrated. This research focuses on managing consistency with a specific set of dependencies called functional dependencies, in addition to handling missing values in databases. We have developed two approaches to handle inconsistencies: a strict one that eliminates all inconsistent entries, and a more permissive one that permits entry inconsistencies while prioritizing data coverage. We have established lower and upper bounds on the number of entry inconsistencies allowed in the latter method, and demonstrated that this method can effectively maintain consistency when incorporating new data, with performance comparable to traditional methods.

This paper introduces a new stochastic process called Time-Dependent Poisson Autoregression (TPAR). TPAR models consist of a parameter $\lambda_t$ that fluctuates over time and affects the autoregressive relationship between Poisson count observations. Unlike traditional Poisson autoregressive models, the process of $\lambda_t$ can change dynamically, potentially leading to complex behaviors such as regime shifts, non-stationarity in parameters, and temporal aggregation effects. Our research demonstrates how the TPAR process can be utilized to analyze and interpret various phenomena by providing statistical properties, an estimation approach using maximum likelihood estimation, and an asymptotic representation of the maximum likelihood estimator.

The task of categorizing and manipulating objects in complex scenes is a key aspect of intelligent robotics, and this work introduces Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs) to effectively represent objects using descriptors. In contrast to traditional methods that rely on explicit registration for object categorization, NDFs use neural networks to directly produce descriptors that capture intrinsic object properties, eliminating the need for explicit alignment. This novel approach is also a natural fit for using SE(3)-equivariant neural networks, which reduces the search space for object categorization and manipulation by considering descriptors' invariance under rigid transformations. NDFs are demonstrated in two applications: categorizing and manipulating objects in 3D point clouds and reconstructing objects from raw RGB-D images. The results show that NDFs outperform conventional methods using registration for both tasks, and the code is available at the public repository.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classic scenarios. Specifically for O(2), O(3), and higher N values, we have determined $z_ c / \xi$ with $\xi$ representing the correlation length and $z_ c$ as the critical amplitude of scaling. Our calculations yielded $z_ c / \xi = 2.70^{+0.01}_{-0.02}$ for N=2, $z_ c / \xi = 2.73^{+0.01}_{-0.02}$ for N=3, and a general formula $z_ c / \xi = 2.70 + 0.03/N$ for N values greater than 3.

In the context of random spin glasses, we have recreated the Sudakov-Fernique curve, which marks the boundary beyond which the AMP method's validity breaks down does not align with the TAP free energy's curvature as previously claimed in [49, 50]. Instead, we establish that the TAP free energy's negative curvature holds only near the optimal solution, defined as the solution with the highest free energy among all possible solutions along the Sudakov-Fernique curve. This optimal solution is unique, has a negative second derivative at a specific point, and contains all the necessary conditions for the validity of the AMP equations.

Astronomical observations, specifically using photometry from the Advanced Photometric Telescopes (APT) at the Mauna Kea Observatory, offer an alternative approach to studying atmospheric aerosol levels. By analyzing how aerosols affect scattering of starlight, this method completes traditional remote-sensing techniques that rely on infrared satellite data, providing independent information about aerosol characteristics such as size and shape. This study leveraged data from the APT system in the Hawaiian Mauna Kea region to study local aerosol patterns and validate the method for deriving aerosol properties from photometry in various astronomical bands.

Recently, deep learning-based pose estimation techniques have gained significant traction, thanks to the widespread use of monocular images. However, these methods often rely on vast amounts of annotated training data, posing a substantial challenge for many applications. In contrast, our proposed DeepHMap++ leverages projection clustering to significantly reduce the required annotations. This approach groups feature projections into distinct clusters to create a compact descriptor, which serves as the primary pose descriptor. Furthermore, we introduce a correspondence learning technique to enhance the robustness of pose estimation by analyzing the distribution of corresponding points. In a series of experiments, DeepHMap++ demonstrates superior performance when working with limited annotations, outperforming comparable methods by a considerable margin. When trained with unrestricted data, DeepHMap++ shows comparable results to the state-of-the-art deep learning-based approach, but with a substantial reduction in model size.

GGLasso is a Python library developed to address diverse Generalized Graphical Lasso problems, encompassing multivariate models with selection of margins, conditional independence, and sparse graph structures. Based on the KoKrMa algorithm of reference [6], GGLasso offers an efficient and flexible framework for solving a broad class of Graphical Lasso optimization problems, leveraging the Python programming language and the SciPy optimization suite. The package's versatility is further highlighted by its capacity to interface with a range of user-provided log-likelihood estimators. Building upon GGLasso's foundations, the paper demonstrates the solution of several specific problems utilizing this framework, including multivariate change point detection and sparse estimation of a bivariate stochastic differential equation.

Accurately modeling configurational temperature effects in molecular simulations is crucial, especially when dealing with complex systems and subtle interactions. Despite the importance of this aspect, most molecular simulation methods, including Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics techniques, often neglect temperature influences on configurational processes. This study presents a comprehensive review of temperature impacts on molecular simulations, specifically examining the effects of configurational temperature on bond stretching and angle bending. Based on the insights gained, a new method is proposed to determine optimal bond lengths and angle parameters by utilizing molecular dynamics simulations in the canonical ensemble. The proposed method also accounts for anharmonic effects and scattering in small molecules. Furthermore, this research demonstrates the practical application of the new method in determining geometric parameters for liquid methane and ethane molecules. The resulting parameters are compared to their harmonic and anharmonic counterparts, obtained through the application of the anharmonic force field to numerical simulations of molecular vibrations.

We have developed a multilayer eigenvector centrality approach that takes into account the variation in node importance across different network layers. This method enables the simultaneous analysis of multiple networks with corresponding node correlations. Taking inspiration from the traditional eigenvector centrality algorithm, we have created a new framework that can be applied to multilayer networks with complex, real-world characteristics. Our research has been demonstrated through a simulation study and real-world data analysis, specifically with regards to co-authorship networks across multiple academic disciplines. Our results have been compared to existing multilayer eigenvector centrality approaches, and have been found to align with the expectations of a contact matrix during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock quantum mechanics predictions for massive 
particles. Here, we develop the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra further to create an $R$-Minkowski 
spacetime, and subsequently derive a massive Dirac equation using this $R$-Poincar\'e 
algebra. The resulting equation exhibits a major difference from its standard form, 
with the rest energy showing up as a fundamental component. Additionally, we solve 
the massive Dirac equation in the presence of an electromagnetic field within this 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime.

A sphere entering water at moderate speeds experiences a complex sequence of events, beginning with a sudden loss of air from beneath the surface as it breaks through the water's surface, followed by air entrapment deep within the sphere as it sinks. This air entrapment persists until the sphere reaches its maximum depth before the air is eventually released. Researchers have extensively studied and debated various aspects of this phenomenon using high-speed imaging. Although previous studies have focused on high-speed impacts where the air remains trapped above the water's surface and on low-speed impacts where the air remains trapped within the sphere for its entire descent, the intermediate speed regime has received relatively little attention. This study utilizes high-speed imaging to investigate the water entry surface seal performance of spheres entering water at moderate speeds, ranging from 2 to 6 m/s. Key observations from the images reveal that the surface seal phenomenon can be divided into three distinct stages, with the duration of each stage influenced by the sphere's velocity. Additionally, the study finds that the intermediate surface seal stage can be further divided based on the relationship between the sphere's diameter and the distance it travels before the air is released from the water beneath it.

We investigate the impact of a specific axion field configuration on the symmetry of a $\mathcal{N}^{16}$ $D=4$ supergravity theory, arising from the reduction of $\mathcal{N}^{8}$ $D=5$ supergravity with a single chiral fermion. Generalizing the $\theta$-term, this field contribution leads to a $\pi_1(M_4)$-dependent effect that affects the reality condition of the supergravity parameters. As a result, this gives rise to a $\pi_1(M_4)$-dependent change in the symmetries of the supergravity theory. We then examine the implications for the consistency of the effective action within the framework of general relativity, specifically in the context of a compact, smooth spacetime.

Our calculations using first-principles methods have identified the unique electronic and magnetic properties of cubanite, a rare mineral composed of copper and iron, and arranged in a complex three-dimensional lattice. This study examined how cubanite's magnetic behavior is influenced by applying pressure and electric fields to its surface. Notably, our findings suggest that cubanite exhibits unusual coexistence of ferromagnetism in its outermost orbitals and antiferromagnetism in its innermost, despite initial indications of conflicting magnetic properties. This paradoxical behavior is further supported by existing experimental data, including the scattering patterns of low-energy electrons and X-rays, and the absorption of X-rays after being excited to high energies.

A type of quantum fluctuation known as Rabi oscillations or "quantum jumps" occurs when a system interacts strongly with external light. Although typically small, Rabi fluctuations can significantly impact the behavior of semiconducting systems in the dark, formed under certain illumination conditions. Researchers have recently discovered giant Rabi fluctuations in a specific dark state of excitons, a coupled electron-hole system, found in a layer of semiconductor material called a quantum well, stacked with another identical layer at a very small distance. This phenomenon arises due to the unique properties of excitons in quantum wells, specifically their dark state, where two layers are connected through a weak energy link. This connection causes fluctuations to synchronize between the two layers, resulting in extremely large Rabi fluctuations. This finding holds particular interest for semiconductor quantum well structures and similar dark-exciton systems in micro or nanoscale environments.

Our investigation focuses on a two-dimensional non-symmorphic wallpaper network lattice made up of carbon atoms on a copper (100) surface. This lattice enables us to create a precisely controlled and chemically pure environment for a single species of atoms. By varying the distance between the copper substrate and the carbon atoms, we can manipulate the energy levels of the lattice. In this study, two-dimensional non-symmorphic wallpaper network lattices are theoretically proposed to exhibit a unique property - a type of band structure known as a Dirac cube. This feature has significant implications for high-speed electronic data transmission and could be realized in this specific lattice design by adjusting the height of the carbon atoms above the copper substrate.

Quantum phases represent distinct patterns of quantum fluctuations in many-body systems and are typically distinguished by ground-state energies or magnetization. However, the concept of coherent phases can be more versatile, encompassing conditions where phases are characterized by different coherent states, beyond the commonly examined Gaussian states. We introduce a proposal to create single-photon catalyzed coherent phases in a cavity with a Bose-Hubbard dimer, utilizing quantum-optical catalysis. When a single photon is used to catalyze the phase, we demonstrate the ability to prepare a Schrödinger cat state, a state with both "0" and "1" photon components, in one of the dimer's sites by adjusting the initial conditions. This results in a phase, where the statistical moment, indicating the number of photons, exhibits quantum fluctuations between two values in the cat state site. This site's population can be mapped to the original superconducting qubit via a Josephson junction, allowing for the detection of the catalyzed phase through current measurements.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in analyzing complex geometries. This review focuses on the fundamental principles and key applications of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, covering both its electromagnetic and Weyl curvature aspects. The paper begins by presenting the basic mathematical framework of the Newman-Penrose formalism before delving into the concepts of self- and anti-self-dual bivectors. It then explores the relationship between the Weyl tensor's conformal decomposition and the G'2 $\oplus$ G'0 complex, ultimately leading to the derivation of the Weyl tensor's index theorem.

A recent advancement in single-cell protein analysis allows the inference of cellular processes, population structures, and immunological responses through the analysis of mass spectrometry data without the need for a reference database. Our contribution builds upon this progress by developing a statistical approach to model polymers in single cells using mass spectrometry data. Unlike previous methods, this approach does not require a pre-existing reference database of known polymers. Instead, it infers the molecular structure of polymers using a combination of linear regression and integer programming. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by applying it to real mass spectrometry data from E. coli, both with a reference database and without one. The results show that the method can accurately reconstruct polymers from their MS data, even in the absence of a reference database.

We developed a novel medical image segmentation technique called Dilated Dense Focus Unet (DDAUnet). This method combines features from both dense and transverse convolutional blocks in its architecture. DDAUnet employs a single-scale approach without using patch-based processing or multi-scale fusion. We applied this method to esophageal tumor segmentation on CT scans, a particularly challenging task due to low contrast and proximity to the esophagus. A public dataset from MICCAI 2017 was utilized for training and evaluation. We also created a custom dataset of 100 CT scans for training and validation. Evaluation metrics on the public dataset showed that DDAUnet ranked 1st among 17 submissions for the MICCAI 2017 task, with a Dice score of 0.856 and a 95th percentile of 0.016 for the Hausdorff distance.

This paper delves into the complexities of code-mixed NLP, focusing on post-neural advancements and multilingual communities. While code-mixed language has been extensively studied from a sociolinguistic and pragmatic perspective, it is less understood from a computational perspective. This paper explores the reasons behind this gap, examining the societal and cultural underpinnings of code-mixed language within multilingual populations. It is argued that code-mixture is a strategic language choice that facilitates communication, particularly in situations where full fluency is lacking. However, this choice introduces challenges in NLP tasks, particularly in identifying the underlying languages. The paper also examines current approaches to handling code-mixed data, highlighting limitations and potential future directions. In the process, it is hoped that this work will encourage more research into code-mixed NLP from both sociolinguistic and computational perspectives.

Human-generated descriptions serve as a gold standard for evaluating image description systems, yet the value of benchmark data comprising human-provided descriptions without a parallel text is also beneficial. Such data can be utilized to educate the language model, conduct numerous generation tasks to create diverse descriptions, and determine a best-fit description for a given image. Human assessment of these descriptions against the gold standard can pinpoint their accuracy and identify areas in need of improvement in the image description system. Furthermore, the cost of creating additional benchmark data is minimal, as it simply entails designating one description from the existing pool of human-generated responses as the standard for a particular image.

We have performed ab initio simulations using both the pseudopotential and full-electron methods to investigate the possible lattice structures of Ta$_2$O$_5$. This material exhibits a phase transition from a high-temperature orthorhombically distorted phase to a low-temperature monoclinous phase. However, experimentally determining its low-temperature state proves challenging due to phase coexistence and sample quality issues. To overcome these difficulties, we have carried out Monte Carlo simulations based on effective models for both phases, and our results suggest that Ta$_2$O$_5$ adopts a $Gd$$_2$O$_3$-type lattice in its ground state.

An in-depth examination of Reddit discussions in the United States during the initial phase of the COVID-19 pandemic has been conducted to analyze the spread of misinformation and vaccine acceptance. This research aimed to explore how demographic changes affecting population mobility influenced misinformation circulation. A significant correlation was found between vaccine acceptance and reluctance in specific Reddit communities, with areas experiencing high migration rates exhibiting lower vaccine acceptance. Furthermore, the study revealed that misinformation about COVID-19 and vaccines was more prevalent in communities from regions with high migration rates. These findings were consistent across various regression models and subreddits. The pandemic's timing, which coincided with the end of the Great Inversion, a long-term migration pattern in the United States, also provided a unique opportunity to assess the impact of the Big Geographic Shift on vaccine misinformation. This phenomenon, characterized by large-scale migration from urban to rural areas, was found to contribute significantly to the circulation of vaccine misinformation, with estimated effects on local communities comparable to those of social media platforms.

Human-robot collaboration through teaching by demonstration relies heavily on effectively interpreting the underlying meaning of instruction sounds made by humans during demonstrations. While prior studies have focused on extracting action details from audio instructions, they have not delved into the fundamental aspects of audio signals that underpin their semantic content. This paper embarks on an in-depth analysis of frequency and temporal characteristics of instruction sounds made by humans during demonstration tasks to robots. It examines how different acoustic elements, specifically pitch, intensity, and duration, are utilized to convey distinct instructional messages across three categories: action guidance, feedback provision, and clarification requests. It also explores the predictive potential of these features in identifying the intended meaning of sounds. A dataset comprising 45 human instructors and 12 demonstration tasks at three difficulty levels is utilized to conduct this analysis. It is found that low-frequency components hold significant importance in interpreting audio structures, whereas pitch and duration patterns are instrumental in distinguishing between positive and corrective feedback. It is also observed that instruction sounds often exhibit a degree of variability, especially in response to task-related queries. This study's findings can serve as a foundation for designing audio interfaces that leverage the inherent properties of human speech for more effective human-robot teaching.

A class of conformally flat metrics is considered in three-dimensional space, resulting in an intricate conformal field theory with a specific set of equations that govern its evolution. Our primary objective is to examine this theory's intricacy by utilizing the Euler-Arnold equation framework, which provides a unifying perspective that encompasses both geodesic surface equations and Euler's topological rearrangement equation as specific instances of its components.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Despite their growing popularity, testing for conversational agents remains a time-consuming and labor-intensive process, largely dependent on human testing to identify defects. Human testing, although effective in simulating real-user experiences, is impractical for large-scale automated development. This paper proposes an automated testing framework that streamlines the testing process for conversational agents using UIML, a markup language for user interface development. The framework's capabilities include verifying interface changes, validating functional properties, and detecting inconsistencies between the system's behavior and intended specifications. The proposed system's flexibility allows developers to incorporate various testing approaches, ensuring seamless integration with existing development methodologies.

Cross-domain recommendation has been a significant area of study lately, as it aims to leverage information from one domain to enhance performance in another. This approach has been particularly useful for businesses operating in multiple geographic regions. However, existing methods often overlook the presence of multiple sparsity domains, which can hinder model performance by contributing to item and user shortages. In response, we propose a novel approach called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR) that addresses multiple sparsity domains in addition to traditional item and user sparsity. By incorporating multiple sparsity domains, our approach can select the most valuable domains to enhance model performance while mitigating the effects of item and user sparsity. To handle item and user sparsity, we develop a novel framework called Comprehensive Aspect Preference Learning (CAPL), which combines top-N recommended items and incorporates a neural collaborative filtering component to enhance the preference learning process. Through extensive experiments on real-world datasets, our approach achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Hypatia.jl is a Julia package that solves convex equations using second-order conic functions. These conic functions encompass a range of mathematical operations including matrix positive semi-definiteness, matrix absolute norm, and geometric mean of matrices. Hypatia.jl leverages the MOSEK solver to achieve this capability. The package enables users to define variables as various conic functions and then formulate equations using these variables. Once the equation is defined, Hypatia.jl can be used with the MOSEK solver to check if the equation has a solution, find a solution, or determine the closest solution. The package also offers an interactive command-line interface for testing and validating the conic equation solutions.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a non-invasive medical imaging technique used to create detailed pictures of the brain, allowing healthcare professionals to diagnose and monitor neurological conditions. To achieve high diagnostic accuracy, MRI scans must be performed and processed correctly, which can be influenced by various factors including the MRI machine used, the operator, and the processing software. As a result, the quality of MRI scans can vary significantly, posing a challenge for artificial intelligence (AI) models designed to analyze brain images automatically. In a study published in the journal Medical Image Analysis, researchers demonstrated how a deep learning model can be trained to generalize across different MRI machines, operators, and processing software, even those not seen during training. The model's effectiveness was evaluated using real-world data from multiple centers, and the findings showed that it can successfully apply the knowledge gained to new, unseen MRI quality assurance problems. The research provides a framework for developing robust, universally applicable brain MRI quality assurance protocols using deep learning.

The integration of private electric vehicles in a smart charging system can either aid in stress reduction for the power distribution network or contribute to its resilience issues, depending on factors like charging schedules and vehicle usage patterns. This study develops a multi-agent optimization framework that considers private EV owners as individual agents with distinct objectives, including minimizing costs and maximizing convenience, while a central manager prioritizes network resilience. The study examines various scenarios to assess the impact of private EVs on network resilience and investigates the effectiveness of management strategies in reducing stress on the network. The results show that private EVs can pose a significant threat to network resilience, and effective management through smart charging is crucial to mitigate this issue. The research also highlights the importance of considering private EVs in grid planning and the need for policies that promote charging during off-peak hours.

The underlying assumption in traditional game theory is that agents act rationally to maximize their payoff. However, real-world interactions involve elements of motivation, as seen in meetings where multiple agents collaborate to achieve a common goal. In this context, we develop a new framework that models meetings among multiple motivated agents, whose state of mind evolves over time in response to input and internal drives. Unlike previous approaches, this framework bypasses utility maximization, instead using reinforcement learning to determine policy functions that map the agents' state of mind to actions and drives. We demonstrate the practical applications of this model in two scenarios: a simple example with two motivated agents and a more complex case of a meeting with three agents, where the task is to discuss and agree on a common topic.

Recently discovered GdSn3 and CmSn3 compounds exhibit unique properties, with GdSn3 displaying ferromagnetism below 100 K and CmSn3 showing itinerant electron magnetism. To further explore these features, we conducted a comprehensive study using first-principles calculations within the framework of the generalized gradient approximation plus Hubbard U method. Our results confirm the stability of the A15 crystal structure for both compounds and align with experimental lattice parameters. We also obtained energy bands and orbital occupations as well as magnetic moments of around 2.5 $\mu$B for both GdSn3 and CmSn3. To facilitate experimental realization, we investigated the possibility of growing GdSn3-CmSn3 solid solutions through partial substitution of Gd with Cm. Our findings suggest that a 10% Cm substitution maintains the A15 structure and preserves the ferromagnetic ordering, with a notable increase in magnetic moment to 3 $\mu$B.

Using the Dyson-Schwinger equations and their non-perturbative solutions for quark and gluon propagators in Landau gauge, we have derived predicted properties for hypothetical additional QCD fundamental fields. These properties include predicted mass ranges, effective masses, and impacts on chiral symmetry breaking. We have specifically analyzed the predicted effects for additional quark flavors, scalar quarks, axial vector quarks, and meson-meson bound states. Furthermore, we have compared our predicted mass ranges to those from other approaches, such as the " Veneziano formula" and "Polyakov loop" effective theories.

In 1980, Hohlweg and Mueller-Prohme established a significant link between the elements of the nth order binary reversible dihedral group and the rational function field over the rational function field K(t) with a specific property. This property requires that every non-constant polynomial within the field has degree exactly n for its leading coefficient. Building upon this work, we have generalized a fundamental theorem to include the bianary Coxeter groups of type B, for the first time in this context.

Type Ia Supernovae (SNe Ia) serve as a primary cosmological distance indicator due to their predictable brightness variability. However, a persistent, yet unexplained, dispersion in their maximum luminosity could potentially limit their precision. One possible explanation for this variation is the presence of a nearby, gravitationally lensing object, which would amplify the SNe Ia's brightness and mislead it into appearing more luminous than it actually is. We have developed a new method to identify such cases of lensing amplification around SNe Ia using the Pantheon SN Ia sample and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). By cross-matching SN Ia and galaxy positions within the same sky area, we have created a model of lensing magnification that can be applied to the observed galaxy populations. We have further developed a statistical approach to remove biased lensing effects on SN Ia samples by integrating the likelihood of lensing amplification in the observed magnitudes. We have applied this method to the Pantheon SN Ia sample and found a median increase of 0.05 magnitudes in the dispersion of the standard Hubble diagram, although the result shows significant variability when considering different galaxy populations. We have also tested our method using mock data sets and found that it successfully recovers the expected results.

We investigated T-shaped photonic junctions within a silicon-on-insulator medium and found that they can form nodes for certain light waves. Our research utilized the time-domain finite-difference time-domain method to simulate T-junctions and revealed that specific configurations give rise to light nodes at the T-shape center. Notably, we discovered that T-junctions can create light nodes in multiple dimensions and that these nodes can be adjusted by modifying the T-shape's geometry. Our findings also showed that T-junctions with a 180-degree phase shift at the cross-over point can form optical nodes even in bulk materials.

Context is a critical component that informs object detectors about a scene's overall information, enabling them to focus on relevant regions and prioritize detection tasks. Despite its significance, evaluating context remains a subjective task that relies on human judgment, hindering the development of objective performance metrics. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach based on saliency maps that assesses context by measuring the attention objects divert from their natural path of detection. This method allows for both human-interpretable and quantitative evaluations of context, which we demonstrate enhances the effectiveness of training deep object detectors using reinforcement learning. Our findings show that context assessment stands out as a critical performance indicator, particularly when detectors are challenged with multiple objects in a single scene. To facilitate reproducibility, we provide the code and models used in this research at the corresponding website.

Additionally, we assume that $|x|^{2}f_i(x,u_1,\ldots,u_k)\in L^1(\Omega)$ for $i=1,\ldots,k$. We derive new concentration inequalities for sums of random variables with binary outcomes, where the variables can be either positively or negatively correlated with each other. Our main result shows that for a sequence of random variables with negative pairwise correlations, there exists a data-driven way to choose $\lambda_j$ such that the concentration inequality for their sum can be expressed in terms of the variance of the sum and $\lambda_j$ as itsenlargement factor. This is in contrast to the standard approach where the concentration inequality for negatively correlated variables is obtained using the Talagrand's concentration inequality on the hypercube, resulting in an inequality with variance as its second-order term. Our method of proof relies on a new application of the pre-Posteriori theorem to the George-Treichel version of the Bounded Differences inequality.

We establish that a symplectic transformation represented by a matrix can be converted into an equivalent form using a specific type of transformation, which we call a "standard conjugation". This standard conjugation is achieved through a sequence of three successive operations, each involving a simple rotation about one of the coordinate axes. We further demonstrate that any two proposed equivalents of a standard conjugation, which yield the same original and modified matrices, will ultimately lead to the same result after simplification.

A key challenge in kidney allocation systems arises when more people require a kidney transplant than donated kidneys are available. To address this, a priority system has been proposed that considers two main tiers: a "match pool" for easily matched donated kidneys and a "stretch pool" for harder-to-match kidneys. However, the question remains of how many kidneys from each pool should be accepted to maximize transplant success. In this research, we develop mathematical models to analyze both first-come-first-served and priority allocation systems for harder-to-match kidneys. Notably, we demonstrate that accepting more "stretch pool" kidneys may lead to a decrease in transplant opportunities, potentially harming those at the lower end of the waiting list. This finding contrasts with the prevailing assumption that accepting more of these kidneys benefits those at the upper end of the list. Our findings also highlight the significance of estimating the size of the waiting list in order to make informed decisions about kidney allocation.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive analysis of the two primary word embedding models, Word2Vec and GloVe, to understand their comprehension of the terms associated with financial text's emotional intensity, as defined by the Loughran-McDonald dictionary. By conducting a series of experiments, we utilized both supervised learning and hyperparameter tuning to create predictive models that can identify the polarity of words from their embedded representations. Our findings reveal that while these models excel at predicting word polarities, their performance is significantly influenced by their training data and choice of architecture. Notably, we discovered that neither model accurately distinguishes positive and negative words in the mid-range intensity levels. Furthermore, our analysis of the geometric structures of the word embeddings reveals a non-intuitive segregation along a single axis, with the embedded representations of extremely positive and negative words converging in the middle range. To facilitate further research, we have made available both the code and pre-trained models for the tasks studied.

This research develops SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM transmission techniques as simplified variants of a previously proposed WF-ICED framework. The WF-ICED approach, presented in our prior study, involves a single integrated baseband system that optimizes combined data and energy transmission under various constraints. The current study focuses on SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems without power splitting, treating the WF-ICED concept as a reference. Building on this reference, we create SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM counterparts by modifying the WF-ICED design. The resulting SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems outperform their conventional counterparts in terms of spectral efficiency.

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we develop a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representations. This method is demonstrated through simulations of melting problems, mushroom growth, and Stefan problems with Dirichlet boundary conditions.

In complex multiplayer games with multiple agents, finding an equilibrium strategy can be challenging, especially when relying on reinforcement learning without explanations. This issue is compounded by the vast number of possible equilibria, many of which may be unstable or difficult to achieve. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel framework that leverages federated multi-agent reinforcement learning with explanation APIs to efficiently identify the most relevant equilibria. This approach is enabled by a new concept called a "learnable endgame," which represents a simplified, shared mental model of the game's final stages. By focusing on the endgame, the number of possible actions is significantly reduced, allowing for a more efficient learning process. Our approach is designed to accommodate partially observable games and incorporates techniques to handle issues of reference frames and co-ordination. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a range of multi-agent game benchmarks, including simple scenarios and more complex applications like traffic management.

An intriguing model that combines network epidemiology and random graph theory has been proposed in this study. According to this model, infected nodes are immediately removed from the graph, and healthy nodes connect to sources of new infections rather than existing healthy nodes when they become infected. By taking a stochastic process approach, researchers have derived an exact expression for the expected number of infections in the limit as the epidemic's duration becomes infinite, and they have also established that this result transitions from a sudden onset of an epidemic to no epidemic as the epidemic's duration crosses a threshold that depends on specific network characteristics.

A comprehensive framework for PDF fitting has been developed to accommodate the
intricate relationships between parton distribution functions, relevant processes,
and experimental data. This framework, tailored for the Drell-Yan dataset at the
LHC, incorporates a novel approach to incorporate semi-analytical Monte Carlo
simulations of scattering processes. A key aspect of this framework involves the
integration of partonic cross-sections, parton distribution functions, and process
weights into a unified operator that facilitates efficient computation of weighted
MC coefficients. Furthermore, this framework enables the implementation of custom
process weights, as well as the incorporation of process-specific corrections and
acceptance modifications. A modular design allows for the seamless integration of
new processes, corrections, and acceptance criteria. A benchmark study using the
Drell-Yan dataset at the LHC highlights the significance of process weight tuning
and highlights the framework's versatility in accommodating various processes and
corrections.

Reinforcement learning's effectiveness can be significantly enhanced through the use of experience replay, which enables policies to be trained on diverse sets of data across multiple iterations. However, the current approach, which involves uniformly sampling episodes for policy improvement, has a major limitation - it fails to account for the disparate levels of variance in returns across episodes. This variance can either positively or negatively impact policy improvement, depending on its magnitude. Inspired by the variance reduction techniques used in stochastic optimization, we propose a non-uniform sampling approach to diminish the variance of return estimates, thereby facilitating faster policy improvement. This Variance Diminution Experience Replay (VDER) method leverages multiple distinct return estimates from sparse data and selects the middle return values from sorted lists, effectively reducing the variance of return estimates to a desired level. We further investigate the optimal variance of return estimates for various policy optimization tasks and demonstrate the VDER approach's efficacy by integrating it into state-of-the-art policy optimization methods, resulting in improved performance on a range of challenging benchmark problems.

In our proposed research, we create a new, complex dialogue dataset called MultiTalk, consisting of 2,000 conversation sessions with four participants each. This dataset stands out from existing datasets, as it features intricate, multi-way branching conversations that involve multiple individuals engaging in various sub-conversations with different partners. Unlike simpler dialogue datasets that prioritize one-on-one interactions, MultiTalk is designed to accommodate diverse conversations with multiple branches, presenting a significant challenge for current state-of-the-art models. To evaluate our proposed model against this challenging dataset, we developed a rigorous evaluation metric that assesses the model's ability to produce diverse, branching conversations. Our findings reveal that incorporating a diverse set of training conversations significantly enhances the model's performance in multiple evaluation criteria. Notably, our model excels in producing complex conversations with multiple branches, outperforming a strong baseline model by a factor of 2.5. Our research also highlights the importance of addressing diversity in the model's responses, with a 10% increase in diversity leading to a 20% improvement in evaluation scores.

We present a method for conducting rapid N-body simulations in various cosmological contexts, focusing on a specific class of modified gravity theories where the Poisson equation is modified as $
abla \cdot \vec{f} = (3.00 + \delta_3)\left(
abla \cdot \vec{
abla}\Phiight)$, with $\Phi$ representing the gravitational potential. This approach enables efficient simulations of generic modified gravity effects by treating $\delta_3$ as a parameter. We applied this method to create a library of N-body simulations with different $\delta_3$ values, spanning $-0.01$ to $10$, which can be utilized for modified gravity research by supplementing existing codes with a gravitational Poisson solver. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach using the $f(R)$ model, a specific modified gravity theory, and show that it accurately reproduces the same cosmological outcomes as more comprehensive simulations. This rapid simulation method can be a valuable tool for conducting multiple simulations needed for modified gravity parameter estimation through dynamical cosmological evolution, as achieved through the example analysis of our simulations using the Albrethsen et al. method.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This work extends the specific pairing that combines chordal SLE and the natural Gaussian free field on the upper half-plane to all pairings and a broader class of SLE processes on the unit disk, driven by a certain class of Coulomb gases. These extensions enable us to couple each pairing with a suitable SLE process and provide a probabilistic interpretation of the pairings as well as their conformal covariance.

MediaWiki, the software behind Wikipedia and other prominent collaborative projects, serves as a robust foundation for developing customized knowledge management systems. This paper delves into the creation of WorkingWiki, a specific implementation utilizing MediaWiki features to facilitate integrated data, applications, and services to advance scientific research. WorkingWiki differentiates itself from public-facing projects like Wikipedia by providing a private workspace with user-specific data and tool configurations. This document outlines the architecture and available features of WorkingWiki, highlighting opportunities for custom development and potential uses in various contexts.

This study presents a linearized model for predicting flame dynamics in response to external noise, based on an active control approach that considers flame response as a means of noise reduction. The model is applied to a specific turbulent jet flame, and predictions generated using the active control approach are compared to those produced by a linearized flame response model. The results demonstrate that the active control approach can effectively suppress heat release fluctuations and temperature in the flame, and the effectiveness of this method varies depending on the amplitude of acoustic forcing. Furthermore, the study highlights the potential of the active control approach as a means of explaining why large-amplitude flames often exhibit reduced response to acoustic forcing.

We investigate the impact of neutrinos meeting ultralight dark matter on both ultra-low-energy double beta decay and cosmological research. In the scenario where dark matter has a monopole moment, it would result in a non-zero neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude, potentially detectable by future experiments like C-GT if neutrinos have a mass in the 10 to 50 meV range. However, even with improved measurements of the effective number of neutrino species, a specific combination of cosmological parameters would remain ambiguous due to uncertainty in the Hubble constant. This ambiguity could be resolved with a more precise determination of the dark matter mass or a detection of the 21cm signal from the cosmic dark ages.

Nonlocal gravity represents a novel, classical approach to general relativity, characterized by the introduction of a nonlocal connection that serves as the fundamental geometric entity. This connection is distinct from both metric and affine connections commonly found in general relativity. We examine nonlocal gravity through a nonrelativistic, semi-classical perspective and demonstrate that the nonrelativistic limit of nonlocal gravity is directly linked to nonlocal Newtonian gravity. Furthermore, we establish a nonlocal Poisson equation that governs the nonrelativistic limit in nonlocal gravity. This framework encompasses both nonlocal gravity and nonlocal electrodynamics as specific cases. We also derive a nonlocal Maxwell-Proca equation from nonlocal gravity and demonstrate that it is equivalent to the nonlocal electromagnetism equation obtained through a different approach based on the Minkowski spacetime nonlocality.

A recent surge in accessible data has enabled a comprehensive examination of genome-wide association studies across multiple traits. In this study, we combined 18 previously analyzed traits for 14 different human conditions through genome-wide association studies. These conditions include autoimmune, metabolic, and cancer-related diseases such as type 2 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, and prostate cancer. We identified associations between 1,529 distinct genomic regions and these 18 traits. Notably, certain genomic regions are linked to more than one trait, with 24% of these associations being novel. We also observed a correlation between the frequency and impact of trait-associated variations, with 54% residing in gene-rich regions and 25% impacting gene expression. Furthermore, we found that the majority of disease-associated variations occur in non-coding regions outside of gene-rich areas, with 71% influencing expression levels in nearby tissues. These findings provide a comprehensive foundation for understanding the complex interconnections between multiple human conditions and their underlying genomic mechanisms.

The ATLAS and CMS experiments at the CERN LHC have access to three minor streams: long-lived neutral hadrons, strange and charm baryons beyond the ground state, and excited baryons of the first and second generations. This paper discusses opportunities for discoveries and precise measurements in these areas, leveraging full Run 2 and early Run 3 data. For long-lived neutral hadrons, with lifetimes between 0.2 ps and 100 ps and energies exceeding 300 GeV, the main focus is on improving existing searches and developing new strategies. For unusual baryons, with precise measurements of their properties, the key is to enhance acceptance and reduce mistagging. For excited baryons, with particular interest in the orbital and radial excitations of lambda baryons, the main goals are to study decays into two-body channels and determine form factors via leptonic modes.

We investigated the recurrence times of X-ray bursts from neutron star binary systems and their relationship to their underlying luminosity. Previous research suggested a connection between these times and a specific threshold luminosity, possibly indicating that some neutron stars in binary systems might be hidden above a accretion disk and thus exhibiting pulsation. However, our findings show that even after removing fake pulsars, the distribution of recurrence times in most systems still exceeds the expected times based on their underlying luminosity, suggesting that many of these systems do not exhibit pulsars. Furthermore, we found that the most persistent systems have recurrence times similar to their luminosity periods, potentially indicating that some neutron star binary systems might be undergoing magnetic accretion and thus exhibiting pulsation. Our study focused on six quiescent X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre and found that four of these systems have recurrence times similar to their luminosity periods, and are thus likely undergoing persistent emission similar to the four well-known persistent neutron star binary systems in the Galaxy.

The performance of transition metal dichalcogenides is highly dependent on their atomic arrangement and bond lengths, which can be altered by both lattice vibrations (phonons) and magnetic interactions (spin). Researchers have primarily focused on static interactions where a specific spin state corresponds to a particular atomic arrangement, but there is a lack of understanding about the impact of dynamic interactions where the relationship between spin and lattice configuration changes over time. This study uses theoretical models to examine the effects of both electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions in two-dimensional materials, specifically tungsten diselenide, and demonstrates the potential for these interactions to significantly influence the direction of magnetism and lattice distortion over time. The results also reveal that the performance of these materials in high-frequency applications could be compromised due to the large amplitude of phonons under high drive, but may also exhibit unusual nonlinear behavior.

Natural Language Inference (NLI) is a widely used task to evaluate the semantic understanding of language models. In a standard NLI setup, models are trained on three categories: entailment, contradiction, and neutral statements. However, this variety can hinder the quality of models generalizable to real-world dialogue applications. Real dialogues rarely contain NLI statements with a "neutral" label, which can lead to undesirable outcomes when interacting with language models. In response, we introduce a new NLI variant, called Binary NLI (B-NLI), which omits the neutral category. We also provide a publicly accessible dataset for B-NLI, generated from real dialogue transcripts. Our findings suggest that models trained on B-NLI tasks yield better results than those trained on the standard NLI, particularly when evaluated on a dialogue-based task.

Simulations of rotating low-mass stars have shown that once a certain critical rotation rate is exceeded, mass loss through the stellar surface occurs, potentially affecting the formation and evolution of low-mass, rapidly rotating stars. Despite this impact, research on sub-stellar objects is limited due to their rarity and the limited age of the universe. As such, sub-stellar objects are often modeled as non-rotating bodies in astrophysical simulations. This study aims to fill this research gap by numerically solving the equations of hydrodynamics and heat transport for rotating sub-stellar objects using the method of short-characteristic approximations, and we have performed a comprehensive analysis of simulations for objects with masses between 0.01 and 0.08 times the mass of the Sun at various surface temperatures and rotation rates. Our results indicate that below a certain surface temperature (approximately 2500 K), rapid rotation does not significantly affect the evolution of these objects. However, at higher surface temperatures, rapid rotation leads to mass loss through the surface, and we have established an upper limit for this phenomenon based on energy. Furthermore, our simulations suggest that only objects with masses above 0.03 times the mass of the Sun can maintain a hydrostatic core, and we have also investigated the effects of surface convection on the evolution of these objects.

The technique of amplitude analysis in hadron decay studies is both powerful and
practical. However, this method's effectiveness is dependent on a thorough
understanding of various experimental aspects that can influence final results.
In this review, key sources of uncertainty in amplitude analyses are examined,
with particular emphasis on techniques used in recent studies of three-body
decays. We also discuss the implications of time-independent amplitude analyses
on specific properties of particles and discuss the opportunities for progress
in this area, including the potential benefits of improved modeling of detector
responses and more sophisticated statistical methods.

A new model for GRB afterglows has been proposed, which distinguishes itself 
from previous models by incorporating a significant deceleration period in 
the early stages of expansion for fireballs. This model successfully bridges 
the gap between the radiative and adiabatic afterglow phases and offers a 
unified explanation for various observed phenomena, including the onset of 
radiation, fireball deceleration, and the peak frequency of the radiated 
electromagnetic spectrum. By accounting for both radiative and adiabatic 
components, this model provides specific fitting formulas for observed 
electromagnetic properties, including flux, frequency, and energy. These 
formulas are derived through numerical integration and are validated through 
comparison with existing models, demonstrating good agreement. This new model 
also predicts distinct observational features in multiple electromagnetic 
bands, including high-energy gamma-rays, optical, and radio frequencies, 
and offers insights into the fireball's physical properties, such as its 
radius, energy, and magnetic versus relativistic energy. By incorporating 
both radiative and adiabatic components, this model bridges the gap between 
these phases and provides a comprehensive explanation for observed GRB 
afterglow phenomena.

Bipartite graphs represent a fundamental class of non-weighted graphs, where the vertices are divided into two distinct color classes, and edges only connect between different color classes. This note focuses on the study of a specific graph transformation task known as bipartite vertex splitting, where an isolated component from one of the color classes is merged with a subset of adjacent nodes from the other class to form a new super vertex. Our main contribution is to develop an exact algorithm for the bipartite vertex splitting problem that runs within the parameterized time of the maximum number of isolated components, specifically O(2^p \log p), where p denotes this problem-specific parameter.

This paper explores the potential benefits of using thrusters in a bipedal robot's ankles to improve locomotion efficiency and stability. Based on previous research, a comprehensive analysis through power flow diagrams highlights the potential gains in mechanical energy return and reduced center of pressure variability using ankle thrusters. To validate these predictions numerically, a simulation model incorporating the effects of ankle thrusters on balance control and energetic efficiency is presented. The results from this model demonstrate enhanced energetic efficiency, a more stable gait, and increased robustness to external disturbances. To achieve practical implementation, a feasible design for ankle thrusters is proposed, and a control strategy for the bipedal robot incorporating thrusters is developed through a linear quadratic regulator method.

We define a particular type of valued domains, which we call "total" and they possess a unique divisorial ideal for every valuation. These domains are then categorized into three groups: one with a single divisorial ideal, type I, and two types based on Krull dimensions, type IIa and IIb.

Operating systems have traditionally managed CPU performance by adjusting frequency and voltage in response to workload changes. However, modern processors have complex multi-level cache hierarchies and significant idle times due to memory access, which can limit the benefits of frequency scaling. In this work, we explore the optimal CPU frequency for mobile devices, beyond the typical range of frequency scaling. We developed HyperDegrade, a novel operating system approach that employs machine learning-based task grouping and efficient interrupt handling to enable efficient CPU frequency reduction. We also created a simulation framework, OSFreqSim, to model and evaluate different frequency reduction strategies. Our results using a custom Android build of HyperDegrade on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 810 demonstrate that efficient CPU frequency reduction can lead to significant energy savings, with a 25% reduction in frequency resulting in a 42% increase in battery life. Furthermore, we investigated various frequency reduction policies and validated the effectiveness of HyperDegrade by deploying it on a real device, observing a 10% decrease in battery life when set to 400MHz.

We introduce a novel twist in the study of classical and welded links through the disentangling operation, dubbed $\sigma$-operation. This $\sigma$-operation takes two links and produces a third link, which represents the combination of the two original links when they share a common component. We demonstrate that the $\sigma$-operation yields an invariant under Reidemeister moves by creating a sequence of moves that disentangles the links. This process involves a specific type of move, the $\sigma$-move, which can be achieved through a series of Reidemeister moves. We establish that the $\sigma$-operation is a fundamental concept that underlies both classical and welded links, and explore its properties by examining the effects of the operation on links that differ by a change in orientation.

We demonstrate how to derive a specific Vassiliev invariant of order three by utilizing the Fox-Hatcher loop, a novel construction based on the fundamental group of a link's complement. This construction generates a specific knot invariant that can be distinguished from all invariants of lower orders through singularities caused by branch points in links, and it possesses order three by exhibiting non-trivial behavior under the 3-fold diagonal braiding.

We investigate a scenario where multiple robots, each with the ability to perform different tasks, are positioned on a grid and strive to accomplish various objectives at specific sites within the grid. Due to their limited computation and communication capabilities, these robots must manage their schedules, tasks, and movement in a strategic manner while exchanging information with each other through a regular network. The aim of this research is to develop a framework for optimizing the completion time of task execution by determining the most effective scheduling and routing policies. We begin by establishing a lower bound on the minimum completion time and then design a centralized, grid-based algorithm that meets this benchmark. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for four-task setups on a specific network configuration, the proposed algorithm achieves the square root lower bound, and this result holds generally for all regular networks.

In Federated Learning, models are trained across a network of remote devices by
a central server that coordinates and aggregates updates from the participants.
One of the significant benefits of this approach is maintaining user data
privacy. Despite this advantage, data privacy remains a critical concern in
FL. In this research, two privacy assaults on Vertical Federated Learning are
created and analyzed. VFL trains a model using only specific relevant data
parameters provided by participants. Two privacy assaults, known as Model Inversion
and Label Switching, target trained VFL models. Model Inversion aims to
reconstruct individual participant data based on the trained model and aggregated
parameters, while Label Switching alters label information to mislead the
model's classification. Both assaults are demonstrated using real-world VFL
scenarios and models, and the associated risks and difficulties in detection
are explored.

Kernel methods in machine learning are highly effective but computationally expensive due to the need to calculate a large positive semi-definite matrix. RFKFF proposes a novel method to estimate a kernel matrix based on data characteristics, bypassing the need for an explicit kernel function. Unlike traditional random Fourier feature methods, this approach generates features that are optimally selected to match the data, resulting in improved performance and reduced computational requirements. RFKFF leverages a non-parametric nearest neighbor estimation to efficiently obtain the necessary information to choose features, eliminating the need to know important details such as input dimensions and maximum covariance. The proposed method is particularly well-suited for real-world applications where data dimensions are vast, e.g. text, images, genetic sequences. Experimental results demonstrate significant enhancements in classification and regression accuracy when using RFKFF in place of traditional random Fourier feature methods.

Given a group $G$ and a family of groups indexed by the elements of $G$, $\{H_g : g \in G\}$, the universal wreath product is defined as the embedding of $G$ into the automorphism group of a family of groups that is isomorphic to $\{H_g : g \in G\}$, such that $\sigma_\gamma \circ \tau_\gamma$ equals the inner automorphism corresponding to $g$ for some $\sigma_\gamma, \tau_\gamma$ indexing the groups $H_g$.

This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions and derives several key results regarding these surfaces under specific curvature conditions. Initially, we establish that positively curved hypersurfaces with constant mean curvature (CMC) and negative mean curvature within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions, up to a specific parameter, are equivalent in metrics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these surfaces with positive scalar curvature and negative mean curvature, above this threshold, possess specific topological characteristics. Additionally, we classify the highest parameterized CMC hypersurfaces with positive scalar curvature within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions, demonstrating that these surfaces are topologically equivalent to a sphere of n+1 dimensions with a removed segment.

A new paradigm in wireless communication systems is emerging, where base stations can be powered and supplied with data using cellular signals, without the need for physical connections, known as simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT). This technology can lead to significant reductions in infrastructure costs and increased convenience. However, the effectiveness of this method depends on the distribution of power and signal in a cellular environment. In this paper, we examine the variables affecting power and signal distribution and investigate how they impact SWIPT services. Specifically, we analyze the impact of path loss, fading, and network load on power and signal distribution. Furthermore, we present a mathematical framework to optimize power and signal distribution in a multi-service wireless network. This framework enables the derivation of optimal transmit powers for each cellular signal, which in turn allows for the efficient placement of SWIPT base stations. This research provides a solid foundation for further studies on the performance evaluation and optimization of cellular networks.

Network vulnerability assessment is a critical task in network analysis, especially for removing malicious nodes in combat operations. Research has focused on measuring and analyzing network robustness using various methods, including percolation and immunization. This study investigates the immunization effect on a specific network model called the Cayley tree and aims to identify optimal target nodes for removal to maximize network stability. By analyzing immunization strategies and evaluating the impact of removed nodes on distant components, we can determine the effects of immunization on a giant component and evaluate the resulting network fragmentation. The study reveals that the most critical nodes to target for removal are those with the highest degree, and a universally applicable rule can be derived to guide immunization decisions.

Next-generation gravitational wave detectors will need a significant improvement in low-frequency noise, particularly in the 40 Hz to 120 Hz range, to enhance astrophysical and cosmological observations. To address this limitation, researchers are exploring new detector configurations within the Hanbridge 40m cavity. A novel concept, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, involves filling the mirror chamber with a fluid of varying density to create a gravitational gradient that acts on the interferometer arms. This gradient can be modulated using a sloshing liquid, potentially isolating a new signal channel for noise reduction. A theoretical analysis of the sloshing-Sagnac design indicates it could offer a 10-fold increase in frequency sensitivity within the 40-120 Hz range, and a 3-fold increase in overall sensitivity at higher frequencies.

Recent advances in Massive MIMO technology have led to the development of eXtra-Large MIMO (XL-MIMO) systems with a large number of base station antennas, exceeding 100. These systems offer improved data transfer rates and better resistance to signal interference. In XL-MIMO systems, base stations can simultaneously transmit multiple packets to devices in the vicinity, provided that the packets' coverage areas do not intersect with each other. This property creates a non-overlapping area around each transmitted packet, known as the "visibility region." Researchers have examined various XL-MIMO access protocols in recent years but have primarily focused on circular visibility regions. In contrast, this study delves into the theoretical analysis of protocols based on non-circular visibility regions, with a focus on random access systems. By modeling the XL-MIMO visibility regions as "W-angles," this research aims to explore the optimal protocol configurations that maximize data transfer rates in random access systems.

Recent high-resolution observations in the millimeter and submillimeter wavelengths have revealed that the vertical shear instability in young stars' disks should have a significant impact on their morphology. To better understand these findings, we used a three-dimensional radiative hydrodynamic simulation of a gas and dust mixture and relabeled the data as if observed at 870 $\mu$m with a resolution similar to that of the ATLAS. By comparing simulated observations with characteristics similar to the ATLAS and ALMA's 870 $\mu$m resolution, we identified several prominent substructures in VSI disks that should be observable. Combining these observations with various noise levels and considering the beam sizes of different telescopes, we generated sets of mock observations that can be used to test the detection methods and algorithms for substructures in VSI disks. Based on our mock observations with a noise level comparable to that of the ATLAS, we found that the detection of VSI in solar-like stars would be extremely difficult. However, ALMA's high-resolution observations should be able to detect VSI in VSI disks with larger radii and more prominent substructures, particularly in the form of VSI-induced spiral arms and ridges that extend from these arms to the disk's center.

Recent research into the structure of the neutron skin of lead has been highly influential, thanks in part to precision measurements made possible by the CRIB experiment at the J-PARC center in Japan. This experiment along with other similar measurements made possible by advanced parity-violation measurements at the Brookhaven National Laboratory's Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider have enabled scientists to achieve a level of precision in the calculation of neutron skins of heavy elements, specifically around 60-100 protons and neutrons. This breakthrough has significant implications for the study of neutron stars as it has shown that the study of finite nuclei and neutron stars can be studied in tandem. Specifically, researchers have discovered that the study of finite nuclei can be used to infer the correct density-dependent interaction, which in turn can be used to accurately calculate the density of heavy neutron-rich matter, which in turn can be used to calculate the crust thickness of neutron stars with a precision of around 1 km. This breakthrough has significant implications for the study of the structure of neutron stars, specifically around their maximum mass and the possibility of neutron stars and black holes merging.

We investigate the performance of a type of quantum gate called the Molmer-Sorensen gate under imperfect conditions, specifically when there's a mismatch between the target qubit and multiple background qubits coupled to motional modes, and when the gate is executed at a frequency different from its designed frequency. Our findings show that the gate's fidelity decreases with an increasing frequency shift and stronger coupling to the background qubits. To enhance the gate's stability, we propose using multiple background qubits with carefully adjusted coupling strengths to the same motional mode. This setup allows us to operate at a higher gate duration while maintaining the same level of qubit loss, thus improving the gate's overall performance. Our results also demonstrate that implementing a $\pi$-pulse middle-time Molmer-Sorensen gate at an odd multiple of half the motional mode's period can significantly increase the gate's tolerance to frequency shifts, ultimately making it a valuable tool for universal quantum gate sets.

Our proposed research aims to explore a novel concept of a strongly correlated Dirac metal, driven by both theoretical prediction and experimental verification, with the ultimate goal of discovering a centuries-old postulated particle called the "neutral meson". To achieve this, we will create and characterize a 2D honeycomb-based strongly correlated electronic system, utilizing both theoretical modeling and experimental data from neutron scattering off hydrogen atoms. This system will exhibit topological and non-Fermi liquid properties, leading to predictions of specific scattering patterns that match experimental findings. To further validate our predictions, we will also develop a theoretical framework that combines quantum Monte Carlo methods and renormalization group techniques to analyze the metal's behavior in its most highly correlated state.

Researchers explored the capabilities of the NA62 experiment at CERN to enhance restrictions on a specific parameter in the Standard Model, specifically related to the interaction between a particular lepton and heavy neutral particles. By analyzing the process of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$, they determined the present limit can be set at $2\times 10^{-6}$ for a particular lepton interaction with a mass of 125 MeV, and they anticipate NA62's upgraded detector to raise this limit to $0.36\times 10^{-6}$ after collecting 5 times the current sensitive $K^+$ decays. Using data from hadron therapy, they also assessed the risk to leptonic $K^+$ decay measurements.

Recent advancements in neural sequence generation models have led to a decline in the usage of $N$-gram language models. Despite this trend, our investigation reveals that there's a hidden interest in $N$-gram models within specific neural model applications. In particular, we discovered that many neural models pretraining datasets, including WebText and CLOTHES, contain training datasets that utilize $N$-gram models as a component. To address the limited knowledge about these hidden datasets, we conducted an experiment where a neural sequence generation model was trained using a residual learning approach on STAGe. Our results showed significant improvements over the original text generation task using a single neural model, with a particular highlight on the strong performance of BPE-based models. To further explore the effectiveness of this approach, we created a search tool called GramSeek to analyze the $N$-gram models employed in various neural training datasets.
