We establish that the category of finite-dimensional representations of a quantum group U_q(cl(G)) at a generic complex parameter q, exhibits properties analogous to cluster categories. Specifically, we demonstrate that the functor that assigns representations to U_q(cl(G)) can be realized through a periodic endopermutation of the cluster category O_cl(G), when G is a semisimple finite algebraic group of classical type, up to isomorphism induced by the periodic shift.

In a groundbreaking collaboration, researchers from the University of Wisconsin-Madison, University of Pennsylvania, Georgia Institute of Technology, and Carnegie Mellon University have conducted an in-depth examination of the Forsage scam, a complex pyramid scheme built on blockchain technology. By applying reverse engineering techniques, the study's authors have demystified the intricate mechanisms of Forsage, a scheme that has defrauded millions of dollars from unsuspecting victims. Through a detailed exploration of the scheme's code, promotional tactics, and financial impacts, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of Forsage's operation. By delving into the historical development of the project, the researchers have also reconstructed its timeline. Furthermore, the study includes a set of findings related to Forsage's code, promotional strategies, financial effects, code security, and policy recommendations. This study's findings are presented in a conference focused on blockchain security.

We have conducted a photometric investigation of 19 previously proposed globular cluster candidates located within the inner regions of the Milky Way bulge using near-infrared data from the VVV survey. By creating color-magnitude diagrams using VVV data, we were able to identify three clusters whose characteristics matched those of globular clusters. However, for the remaining 16 clusters, their properties were found to be more consistent with young bulge populations rather than traditional globular clusters. A 3D galactic model was utilized to determine the positions of these 16 clusters, which were found to reside in a specific region associated with a molecular complex that may have contributed to their formation.

In the context of MERA, a holographic tapestry that stores and retrieves information through quantum correlations, we can define "hyper-invariant" subregions that maintain their information encoding capabilities under arbitrary unitary transformations. Our research demonstrates that hyper-invariant regions in MERA, characterized by specific entanglement spectra, resemble the "braiding" patterns found in topological quantum systems and possess a property of holonomic error correction. Furthermore, we can generate a class of hyper-invariant regions around specific holographic codes, which serve as error-correcting codes in the quantum regime. These codes exhibit a peculiar behavior in which the accuracy of information retrieval scales with distance from the code's center in a power-law manner.

Deep-learning methods have recently been applied to process mining, a statistical technique that extracts valuable insights from business processes by analyzing data. In the context of external process discovery, where processes are inferred from data about completed tasks, we compared three advanced techniques using neural networks: Graph Convolutional Networks, Graph Attention Network, and Reinforcement Learning. To evaluate these techniques, we used two publicly available process datasets and generated comparable datasets from process simulation. Our findings show that process datasets generally yield better results than process simulation datasets when predicting processes. Furthermore, we discovered that process simulation datasets produce more consistent performance when using different deep-learning techniques. To facilitate replication of our study, we have made the process simulation datasets and related code publicly available on GitHub.

This research paper delves into the world of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, specifically the $S^{\sigma}_\omega$ class, whose members exhibit smoothness and decay properties under frequency space modulations. We establish a non-trivial existence result for Bessel potential operators acting on $S^{\sigma}_\omega$ spaces by demonstrating that their kernels must possess smoothness and decay properties, meeting or exceeding $\sigma$ and $\omega$ requirements. Furthermore, this result is utilized to develop criteria for non-degeneracy of Toeplitz operators with symbol $\rho$, which are equivalent to the symbol's derivatives and multiple extensions vanishing to infinite order. This in turn leads to the conclusion that the space of Toeplitz operators on $S^{\sigma}_\omega$ is non-trivial if and only if $\sigma > 0$ and $\omega > 0$.

We employed a radiative transfer model in a layer-by-layer fashion to simulate the near-ultraviolet spectrum during a massive flare of AD Leo in 1985, with a significant focus on the continuum. This analysis allowed for a detailed examination of the radiative processes occurring within the atmospheric layers. Our study revealed that the supergranular convective photosphere maintains its standard temperature, yet with a slightly elevated brightness. The simulated continuum revealed a complex behavior, with a notable shift in the formation altitude of the continuum due to the increased filling factor of polarized light within the photosphere. Furthermore, we found that the atmospheric temperature exhibits a significant decrease in the chromospheric layers, with a notable drop in temperature in the upper layers of around 1000 K. This temperature drop is consistent with previous findings based on the H-alpha and Ca II H&K flare spectra.

Point cloud models have gained significant traction in the field of computer vision due to their efficiency and simplicity, particularly in tasks requiring limited computational resources. However, real-world point clouds often contain noise, outliers, and missing data, posing a substantial challenge for the effective training of deep learning models. Existing denoising techniques primarily focus on removing noise from synthetic point clouds generated through random removal of points, which may not effectively generalize to real-world scenarios. In contrast, our proposed method, Transformation-Unique Smoothing (TPC), employs a more realistic noise removal approach by randomly transforming point clouds through rotation, flipping, and shifting before removing points. We demonstrate that TPC surpasses conventional denoising techniques on several real-world datasets in various tasks, including classification, segmentation, and reconstruction. Specifically, our results show that TPC-based training yields better performance than conventional denoising methods in tasks like SHREC13 (median classification accuracy: 73.6%) and the Area Minima Surface (AMS) reconstruction task, also known as surface reconstruction from point clouds.

Using the RPA method, we re-calculated the electric dipole strength distribution for $^{16}$O, with a focus on the giant dipole resonance (GDR) region. Our results show that the standard Lorentzian width overestimates the width of the GDR, and instead suggests a non-monotonic behavior of the GDR's width with increasing energy. Furthermore, we found that the average energy of the GDR remains at approximately 13 MeV, and that the width of the GDR varies significantly with different spin components. Our findings are based on a detailed analysis of the eigenphase shift and Jost function within the RPA framework.

This research introduces a novel approach to clustering nonlinear dynamic systems using time series data, with the primary goal of differentiating systems' impact behaviors. Time series data from a system's output through its evolution over time is utilized, bypassing the need for input data. A dimensionality reduction technique known as Multi-Dimensional Time Series Auto-Encoder (MDTSAE) is developed to extract the most critical features from the data, with a focus on capturing the long-term patterns present across the time series. This method enables the construction of a custom similarity measure that reflects the dissimilarity between the long-term patterns of two systems. In turn, this similarity measure is integrated into a clustering algorithm, K-Means, to group the systems according to their output behaviors over time. Experimental evaluations using simulated examples, in addition to real-world data from the Santa Fe Institute, demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in accurately identifying distinct dynamic regimes within a single system and in correctly classifying multiple systems with varying behaviors.

Neural generative adversarial networks have achieved remarkable performance in unsupervised text generation, where a discriminator is trained to distinguish between two datasets. However, existing methods suffer from a significant imbalance between the generator and the discriminator, leading to limited exploration of this model in text generation tasks. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel SparseGAN framework, characterized by a highly balanced and sparse adversarial learning process. Unlike conventional GAN-based text generation methods, SparseGAN employs a more equitable model where the number of trained generator parameters is significantly reduced compared to the discriminator. To leverage this balanced setting, we develop a series of techniques to enhance text generation through a more challenging discrimination task. Experimental evaluations on multiple text generation datasets demonstrate the superior performance of SparseGAN compared to conventional text generation models.

The theory of interstellar panspermia suggests that microbial life could be transported between star systems through comets and meteorites. While this idea is intriguing, verifying this hypothesis poses significant challenges given the limited understanding of extraterrestrial biology and the harsh conditions comets and meteorites experience during interstellar travel. To assess the feasibility of detecting evidence for interstellar panspermia, we examined four scenarios involving comet or meteorite impacts, with varying levels of biological evidence and in different astrophysical contexts. Our analysis focused on the most plausible context: a comet impacting a giant gas planet like Saturn, which could potentially harbor microorganisms within its icy moons without disrupting their biological makeup. To investigate this scenario, we used a simplified model of astrobiology combined with astrophysical and astronomical observations, and considered various detection methods such as spectroscopy, electromagnetic radiation from heated biological material, and biosignatures from the planetary atmosphere. Our calculations revealed that detecting evidence for interstellar panspermia in this specific context might be difficult with current technology, but could become possible with the development of more sensitive detection tools, particularly high-resolution spectroscopy and advanced microwave telescopes, which could potentially indicate the presence of biological material on distant moons.

Animal movement and social behavior can significantly impact disease transmission among wildlife populations. Understanding how animals choose resources and interact with each other is crucial for modeling and predicting disease spread. This study combines two methods to better comprehend the movement and habitat use of a specific species. The first approach, spatial capture-recapture, utilizes capture data to estimate population density and animal movement patterns. The second method, based on resource choice models, examines how animals select resources. By integrating these two methods, we developed a joint model that incorporates both choice and movement information. This integrated model enables the estimation of population density, animal movement, and resource choice parameters simultaneously. Our results showed that incorporating choice information into capture-recapture analysis helped accurately model animal movement and density, and that movement patterns varied by season. This variation in movement patterns was reflected in the estimated seasonal density of animals at different locations. This research demonstrates the benefits of combining capture-recapture analysis with resource choice models and highlights the importance of considering seasonal movement patterns when modeling population density.

Recent advancements in network science have led to the development of multilayer networks, which can effectively represent interconnected systems of various kinds, including technological, biological, and social entities. Within these networks, oscillatory dynamics and synchronization phenomena can be critical components, as seen in neural, genetic, and cardiac systems. We have established a general framework for multilayer networks of oscillators with transmission time delays and have investigated the conditions for transmitting solutions, a concept that allows for the transmission of solutions from one layer to another while maintaining stability. Our research revealed that the stability of these solutions is influenced by the characteristics of the individual nodes within each layer and the corresponding connections between them. Furthermore, we have identified specific conditions for the existence of transmitted solutions in multilayer networks and have demonstrated that these conditions can be met in various configurations of coupled layers. Our results also show that the multilayer framework can be effectively reduced to a equivalent single-layer model under certain conditions, thus providing valuable insights into the conditions necessary for this equivalence to hold.

Given a vector function space, this study establishes the fundamental basis for the Cauchy stress operator, determining necessary and sufficient conditions in terms of functional equations. The operator's parameterization, with its minimal structure revealed, consists of three main components: a scalar multiplier, a symmetric second-order tensor in a linear transformation, and a linear operator that maps vectors to symmetric second-order tensors. This structure serves as both a required and sufficient condition for a valid Cauchy stress operator. The study also explores specific cases of this general framework, including the Biot consolidation theory and the Navier-Stokes equations, among others.

This research focuses on a new testing method for programs that utilizes geometric techniques from computer science, specifically graph theory, Boolean functions, and electrical networks. Unlike traditional testing methods that rely on Boolean functions, this approach leverages the geometric theory of Boolean functions to create test cases and determine the program's correctness. We introduce a basic program testing model and a more advanced version that incorporates the algebraic distance between functions, and analyze the complexity of testing these programs using the number of test cases and their total cost. This results in improved testing efficiency, and we explore specific cases, such as programs with restricted structure, using pseudo-algebraic north-west curves, using convex geometry, and programs based on Boolean satisfiability testing, to demonstrate the applicability of this method.

Consider a finite-dimensional vector space over the complex number field with a defined basis, and a linear transformation acting on this space. We establish that any circle of vectors from this space can be mapped to a circle of corresponding row vectors in the representation of the algebra of polynomials associated with the linear transformation, using the basis mentioned earlier.

Estimating node counts and approximate distances in a network are fundamental tasks with various applications, including routing, resource allocation, and network optimization. These estimates can be achieved through a distributed averaging algorithm using neighbor reports from other network nodes. However, such an approach is vulnerable to manipulation by malicious nodes, which can significantly impair the accuracy of the estimates. In this research, we investigate the conditions under a specific small-world network model can provide reliable estimates with a desired level of precision when faced with a certain number of malicious nodes. Additionally, we establish guidelines for selecting an appropriate giant component size that ensures the desired precision in the estimates. Furthermore, we conduct numerical studies to illustrate the implications of our findings on real-world networks.

Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.
This study introduces a nonparametric approach to estimate short-term queue lengths
without assuming a specific distribution, using probe vehicles as detectors.
A novel method based on combinatorial optimization is developed to estimate
queue lengths within a time window of up to 30 minutes, using data from probe
vehicles, historical traffic data, and estimated travel times from probe vehicles.
The approach does not require estimating probability distributions or specifying
model parameters, and instead leverages a binary decision tree to represent the
conditional distribution of queue lengths.
The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through numerical examples.

In numerical relativity, a significant challenge arises when attempting to apply the conformal transverse-traceless decomposition to a 3D tensor, specifically when trying to solve for the conformal factor and transverse-traceless part of the extrinsic curvature. This issue becomes particularly pronounced when using second-order finite-difference methods or higher-order schemes, especially in problems where the extrinsic curvature is weak and its conformal decomposition is uncertain. Our novel approach, CTTK, addresses these difficulties by bypassing the direct solution for the transverse-traceless part of the extrinsic curvature and instead solving for the full extrinsic curvature tensor. We then apply a projection to obtain the desired conformal-traceless component. Our method is computationally efficient and demonstrates improved stability for certain simulations. We have successfully utilized this method in 3D numerical relativity simulations involving the merger of black hole and neutron star binaries.

Manganese nitride thin films, specifically Mn$_3$NiN, exhibit unique spin-orthodomain wall dynamics at room temperature, characterized by a large Nernst effect signal, particularly in the x-direction. This distinctive feature arises from the absence of an external magnetic field applied in that direction, resulting in the lack of magnetic pinning and thus freely rotating spin structures. This rotation leads to the anisotropic Nernst effect, with the x-component showing a significantly greater magnitude than the y-component. This anisotropic behavior persists even after the application of an in-plane magnetic field, until the field becomes sufficiently strong to induce magnetic anisotropy. This unusual property of Mn$_3$NiN thin films presents a promising opportunity to advance spintronic technology.

User facilities like synchrotrons, nanocrystallization labs, and supercomputing centers support cutting-edge scientific research and provide critical services to a broad user base. To maintain their high performance and meet growing demand, these facilities must integrate automation technologies with their equipment and make their operations remotely accessible. However, developing and integrating control systems, software, and hardware across their vast setups poses significant technical challenges. In response to these difficulties, researchers are turning to AI-powered approaches that utilize machine learning for rapid development and efficient maintenance of their control systems. This paper presents an AI-driven framework for creating high-performance, secure, and easily maintainable remote control systems for complex setups at user facilities. Leveraging machine learning techniques, this framework enables users to rapidly develop robust control systems through simple, intuitive commands based on pre-existing data from similar systems. This approach has been successfully implemented and tested at a nanocrystallization lab, where it improved the efficiency of seed crystal production by enabling fully automated remote operations with real-time monitoring.

We have derived improved differentiability properties for solutions to a non-autonomous obstacle problem, formulated as
$u \in S_{ad}(\Omega),\quad \text{with}\quad \text{F}_x(u(x))\in \mathcal{A}(\Omega,\alpha(x)),\quad \text{and}\quad \text{F}_u(u(x))\in \mathcal{B}(\Omega,\beta(x))$ holds true, where $\alpha,\beta\in (1,2)$ and $\beta<\alpha+1$. This generalizes previous results requiring $\beta\leq\alpha$ and allows for the existence of solutions under more general growth conditions.

We provide a clear description of Serre weights for $GL_2$ via Kummer theory, building on Breuil's initial concept. Specifically, we establish a correspondence between certain cohomology classes and a subset of Serre weights, utilizing Kummer theory for a genus theory of binary quadratic forms. This approach yields a straightforward proof that the set of realized Serre weights is equal to the set of locally constant cohomology classes, occurring in a manner analogous to $GL_3$ results.

We establish a novel second-order mesoscale regularity result for functions defining constant mean curvature curves in higher-dimensional space, relying on the presence of a specific isoperimetric residue and an appropriate Pucci-Sabreski growth assumption. This achievement represents an advancement over a corresponding result from 'Minimal surfaces in higher-dimensional space with bounded mean curvature' by N. S. Forni, where a similar conclusion was proven under the condition of bounded second derivatives. Our current proof for this result differs significantly from Forni's approach, utilizing a parabolic version of the Hölder continuity theorem and a PDE variant of the Gehring-Lehto lemma.

A novel approach has been proposed to precisely control and manipulate damage in composite materials by utilizing genetic algorithms in conjunction with electrical impedance tomography. This method enables the accurate determination of optimal voltage patterns required to achieve specific structural states, taking into consideration uncertainty in sensor data. A numerical model based on the finite element method has been employed to simulate both the tomographic images and mechanical responses of self-sensing composites. A self-repairable composite material model has also been developed to predict mechanical behavior based on damage levels. A proof-of-concept demonstration has been conducted to control and manipulate micro-cracks in a composite material.

Recent research suggests that complex systems often benefit from simple components, a phenomenon observed across biology, physics, and computer science. To explore this concept further, we examine the relationship between component complexity and system performance in artificial neural networks, using a novel training method that modifies the complexity of individual neurons based on their contribution to the network's overall task. Our findings reveal that, on average, there is no significant correlation between the total number of complex elements and a network's ability to accurately classify new data. However, when comparing individual neurons within a network, we observe a mix of results, with some showing a negative correlation between complexity and performance, while others exhibit no such trend.

Hermann Weyl's pioneering work from 1923 laid the groundwork for a tensor analysis within curved spaces. This approach, focusing on geometric objects and their transformations, has become a fundamental framework in physics and mathematics. Our research builds upon this foundation by developing a tensor analysis specifically tailored for high-dimensional Euclidean spaces. This approach maintains compatibility with standard tensor analysis and reveals intriguing connections to Lie group theory.

A theoretical model featuring a new scalar field that interacts with both the top quark and the bottom quark at their weak fundamental levels is proposed. This interaction is achieved through the introduction of two large, nearly equal SU(2) coupling ratios. In the low-energy realm, this particle exhibits unusual properties under flavor transformation, switching from a bottom quark to a top quark. It also demonstrates an unusual affinity for weak interactions, surpassing that of the Higgs boson. This model's characteristics can be distinguished from competing theories through specific phenomenological patterns. This particle's potential manifestations in various experiments are examined. It may couple with the top quark and bottom quark in various ways, leading to distinctive two-body or multi-body decay patterns. This particle's possible mass ranges and its predicted interactions with the standard model particles are calculated using a range of energy levels. All conformal field theory correlations can be determined using the Toda conformal field theory, and this paper delves into the specific case of $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory to detail conformal correlations and identify their underlying structure through conformal transformations. A key discovery in this framework reveals that certain correlation functions can be transformed into a particular set of relationships called Ward identities, which take the form of a system of polynomial equations with rational coefficients. This finding expands on a previous finding in the $\mathfrak{so}(2r+1)$ Toda conformal field theory and presents a new framework for analyzing and classifying conformal correlations according to their underlying polynomial relationships.

We demonstrate that the rational group generated by Coxeter generators, under the condition of finite order 4 for squaring relations, is both automatically rational and naturally ordered. Consequently, its membership problem is effectively solvable. Additionally, this problem can be resolved via a finite sequence of basic queries to a decidable theory that encompasses this group, allowing for problems in this group to be reformulated as first-order logic with a single bound variable.

A non-invasive approach to deciphering a person's walking state through their brain signals is a significant step towards creating more effective neural prosthetics for paraplegia patients. Previous studies using functional magnetic resonance imaging have successfully identified areas of the brain associated with walking, specifically within the motor cortex. However, these methods have limitations when it's necessary to provide real-time control over an individual's walking, either naturally or through a robotic device, due to their low temporal resolution. To overcome these challenges, researchers recorded brain signals directly from the motor cortex using electrocorticogram technology from five healthy individuals while they walked on a treadmill. By applying machine learning algorithms to these signals, the researchers were able to accurately determine whether the subjects were walking or standing, as well as identify two distinct walking states (brisk walking and normal walking) based on different step rates. The findings demonstrate that it's feasible to decode a person's walking state from their brain signals in real-time, and highlight the potential for neural prosthetics that can restore natural control over walking without the need for pre-programmed settings.

We provide a detailed description of right-angled Artin spaces for a given graph, focusing on its expression as a non-positive category and its associated properties, including isometry preservation under reordering of the graph's vertices. Additionally, we establish that if a graph's vertex set can be divided into two disjoint subsets, then the associated right-angled Artin space can be constructed by combining the spaces associated with these subsets, with the condition that the resulting space is equivalent to the product of the spaces associated with the subsets.

Estimating node connectivity in graphs from time series data is a complex task, especially when connectivity changes over time. This paper presents a novel approach that uses a two-layer neural network model to effectively analyze static and dynamic connectivity. In assessing static connectivity, our method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques according to AUC scores on four real-world datasets, including correlations, functional connections in brain imaging, protein-protein interactions, and co-purchasing relationships in customer transactions. Furthermore, our approach successfully reconstructs time-varying graphs that align closely with reference datasets based on mean absolute error and mean squared error metrics.

Biological motion refers to the interpretation of human or animal movement from static figures or low-resolution images, a concept initially proposed by Johansson in 1973. This approach has been extensively applied across various fields, including sports, biology, and psychology, and has given rise to several related topics of study, such as the perception of animated shapes and the recovery of scene geometry. This report outlines a biological motion detection project, where participants were shown a static image of a crowd gradually transforming into moving people, and their task was to identify the figure before movement began. The results showed that people can easily recognize static images of crowds even when they are far away, but struggle with individual figures in the distance unless they are moving.

High-speed computing applications, particularly those on GPUs, often prioritize simple algorithms for rapid operations like matrix inversion. However, more advanced techniques like the Wiedeman and Coppersmith method, although precise, are too slow for high-performance computing due to their complex nature. We have developed a more efficient iterative algorithm based on the Wiedeman and Coppersmith method by streamlining its implementation on GPUs. Our research demonstrates that this algorithm can provide accurate results for matrix inversion through an iterative process with a Hessian matrix, with a low computational cost of approximately 24 GFLOPS. Our findings have been applied to the solution of Hessian matrices in optimization problems using the limited memory quasi-Newton method (L-BFGS) with promising results.

Topological phases in one-dimensional systems have been extensively studied and can be protected by disabling time-reversal symmetry through the application of a magnetic field. However, increasing the dimensionality to two dimensions allows for additional means of protecting these phases, including time-reversal symmetry and spatial symmetry. This work focuses on one-dimensional topological systems that have been laterally extended to two dimensions while maintaining time-reversal symmetry, which we refer to as topological Anderson conductors in a general sense. A $p$-orbital based model is used to create a specific type of topological Anderson conductor in two dimensions, characterized by a random binary disorder. This type of disorder results in a "frustrated" potential that affects different orbital shells in an incommensurate manner. As a result, the disorder's impact becomes commensurate with the underlying lattice of a certain "kagome-like" structure when the ratio of the lattice constants to the wavelength of electrons is minimized. This specific type of topological Anderson conductor is distinguished by its unique phase diagram, which includes both topological non-trivial and gapped phases along with a "weak topological insulator" phase. Weak topological insulators in two dimensions possess a $Z_2$ invariant but exhibit no chiral edge modes in their interior surfaces. Instead, they are characterized by helical edge modes encircling the surface normal on their boundary. This phenomenon of weak topological insulators has not been previously reported.

We introduce an algebraic model consisting of cut networks, which are analogous to string rewritings in abstract algebras. Based on this framework, we establish the equivalence to sequential flowcharts using lambda functions, thereby demonstrating the expressive power of cut networks as a fundamental model of computation.

We've developed a code to efficiently calculate the Higgs production and decay modes in the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model with complex parameters, utilizing the on-shell approach for Higgs fields. This code prioritizes calculations for Higgs production and decay processes at particle colliders, specifically focusing on processes involving two bottom quarks. Due to the complexity of the MSSM, we've optimized the calculations to minimize the need for repeated computations of Feynman diagrams, instead utilizing a set of pre-calculated expressions for various processes. These processes include gluon-gluon to bottom-quark pair, bottom-quark pair to bottom-quark pair, and similar combinations, with all processes being calculated for both CP-even and CP-odd Higgs fields. We've made our code publicly available for further development and research applications.

Contextual linear bandits is a prominent model for online decision making under uncertainty in contextual environments, with numerous applications and connections to other machine learning frameworks. In its standard form, the contextual linear bandit problem relies on a centralized agent that gathers historical data and sets the contextual linear parameter vector. However, in many large-scale and modern contextual linear bandit problems, contextual data cannot be shared due to privacy constraints, making this setup impractical. In this research, we develop a context-free linear bandit algorithm called "Privately Learning Contexts" (PLC), which learns the contextual parameter without knowledge of the context distribution. We establish a sublinear regret bound of O(n^(1/3) \sqrt{T}) for PLC, surpassing the existing bound of O(\sqrt{nT}) achieved through centralized methods. Our results also demonstrate that PLC also achieves the optimal rate of O(\sqrt{T}) in single-context settings.

We appreciate the opportunity to respond to questions and concerns raised by reviewers. Our approach to estimating optimal individualized treatment rules that are robust against distributional shifts is grounded in a data-driven method to estimate the set of plausible population treatment effects. This approach bypasses the need to make assumptions about how the future population's covariates will compare to the current sample. Our results show that rules based on our method have comparable performance to gold standard rules in both simulated data and real-world applications with evidence of distributional shifts. Our approach is particularly beneficial when there are issues with covariate shift, and we propose a strategy to extend this method to multiple covariates.

Our study investigates two approaches to manipulating event shapes by adjusting the minimum pseudorapidity ($\eta$) for accepting charged particles in fully inclusive, non-symmetric, and anisotropic heavy-ion collisions. We utilized the fourth-order elliptic flow coefficient ($v_4$) as a reference to compare two methods of event shape adjustment: one based on the four-particle cumulant correlation and another based on hydrodynamics. Our findings indicate that both methods yield similar results for inclusive spectra but distinct results for elliptic flow ($v_4$). Specifically, the four-particle cumulant correlation method overestimates $v_4$ by approximately 10% when requiring a minimum of three units of rapidity separation ($\Delta\eta \geq 2$), whereas the hydrodynamics-based approach predicts an increase of approximately 17% for the same $\Delta\eta$. Our research also revealed that the influence of $\Delta\eta$ on $v_4$ depends on the initial eccentricity and colliding nucleon energy.

In an interference network with $K$ users, each having a distinct transmission goal, we examine the extremal generalization degrees of freedom (GDoF) gains that can be achieved by using the best power control method versus binary power control. It is proven that the extremal gain from optimal power control compared to binary power control can be significant, reaching $\Omega(\sqrt{K})$ when $N$ users are paired into $K$ "clusters", and it is shown that this gain is bounded above by $O(K^{3/5})$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for any $K$, there exists an achievable solution with a GDoF gain from optimal power control over binary power control of $O(K^{3/5})$, and for any $K$, there are interference networks with $K$ users where the GDoF gain from optimal power control over binary power control is $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$.

This study presents a novel multiple-time-step numerical integration method for simulating complex interactions between individual fluid particles and suspended solids within turbulent flows. Existing approaches often employ a single time step that accommodates the shortest collision duration, resulting in inefficient use of computational resources for large-scale simulations. In contrast, our multiple-time-step method assigns distinct time steps to individual particles based on their sizes and densities, allowing for the most rapidly moving particles to be simulated at shorter intervals. This strategy maintains accuracy while significantly reducing computational costs. To accommodate physical collision times, our method incorporates a novel, second-order semi-implicit integration scheme for particle interactions. This scheme ensures that collisions occur at precise physical times, even when the time step falls below this threshold. Our results demonstrate improved predictive performance and substantial speedup compared to conventional methods, with a 4.6-fold increase in simulation speed for a representative case.

This article presents new findings for the Diophantine equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$, focusing on solutions where $a$, $b$, and $n$ are whole numbers with $n$ greater than $2$. Existing research established that when $n$ exceeds $2$, there are solutions for $a$ and $b$ given specific constraints on $n$. Our contribution is to demonstrate that solutions for $a$ and $b$ can be achieved for all $n\geq 3$, thereby generalizing the earlier condition. Notably, when $n$ is odd, we derive solutions for $a$ and $b$ under the condition $0 < a < b < \sqrt{7^n}$, and when $n$ is even, we obtain solutions with $0 < 7^{n/2}-1 \leq a < b < 7^{n/2}$.

This research focuses on a highly dynamic hopping gait for a bipedal robot, specifically a monopod, which is being tested on various soft and yielding terrains to ensure its safety and efficiency in such environments. To effectively navigate these terrains, the robot's ability to predict and adjust its landing points is crucial, and for this purpose, a precise model of the terrain is necessary. This paper presents a method for creating a terrain model that allows for simulation of the robot's interaction with the ground, taking into account the deformation of the terrain under the robot's weight and the impact of its landing. Using this model, further simulations were conducted to test the robot's performance on different terrains, including the optimization of its landing strategy to minimize the height of its hop.

In this paper, a consistent and flexible framework for describing meson form factors is developed and applied to various types of mesons. This framework, which is based on a quark-confinement model, incorporates two different types of meson structures: those with a significant quark-antiquark component and those dominated by a meson's strange partonic component. Theoretical predictions for meson form factors are obtained using a contact quark-quark effective model and are then compared to experimental data. Our results indicate that this framework effectively accounts for the diverse characteristics of mesons, and our predicted form factors for charmed and strange mesons are particularly notable for their consistency with available experimental and theoretical information.

Organizational frameworks with a hierarchical structure are utilized across various domains including academia, business, and technology. These frameworks facilitate efficient information retrieval, enable effective navigation, and streamline decision-making processes. However, managing large-scale, complex hierarchies poses significant challenges, particularly in regards to their construction, maintenance, and evolution. In this context, traditional methods that employ top-down approaches may struggle to accommodate rapid hierarchy changes and large data sets. To address this limitation, we developed an alternative bottom-up approach called the Hierarchical Clustering Framework (HCF), which leverages clustering algorithms to build hierarchies. This approach offers numerous benefits, including enhanced scalability, improved adaptability to changing data, and the ability to handle high-dimensional spaces. We have applied HCF to a wide range of real-world problems and compared its performance to cutting-edge methods used in machine learning and information retrieval.

Quantum annealing holds promise for efficiently resolving complex optimization tasks, yet the reliability of its implementation is affected by uncertainties and errors in the quantum system. This study investigates the impact of the quantum annealing interval on dynamical behavior during a quench, using a spin-1/2 Ising-like Hamiltonian to model a quantum annealer. The results indicate that a sufficiently small annealing interval is necessary to prevent the formation of competing quantum states that could lead to solution loss. Furthermore, the research reveals that the quantum state after the quench can be characterized by a non-equilibrium spin-1/2 Heisenberg model, whose parameters depend on the annealing interval. This finding is particularly significant for solution loss in 2D exact cover problems, which can be mapped onto a 1D chain of the same Heisenberg model.

Our research focused on a two-dimensional model featuring two bands to better understand the infinite-layer nickelate's superconducting properties. By conducting a rigorous analysis within a $e_{g}$-$t_{2g}$ two-band framework, we found that the infinite-layer nickelate's complex electronic environment can be accurately described by a simplified two-band approach. This two-band model successfully replicates the infinite-layer nickelate's key experimental findings, including pseudogap formation, orbital ordering, and charge or spin instabilities in different doping levels. Furthermore, we discovered that the two-band model exhibits a non-fermi liquid behavior near the charge or spin instability points. By applying a moderate amount of Coulomb interaction, the two-band model reveals that the infinite-layer nickelate's $J$-dependent screening effect plays a crucial role in either the Mott-Hubbard or Kondo-lattice picture of physics. This is particularly evident in the $J$-dependent pseudogap formation and the infinite-layer nickelate's tendency towards a non-fermi liquid state. This finding is also consistent with $J$-dependent effects observed in other nickel-based materials systems.

The structure of dense matter within the density range of $3-10$ times nuclear saturation density remains poorly understood, which in turn limits our comprehension of compact and strange stars. While the presence of deconfined strange matter could significantly impact the sound speed, models of dense matter based on relativistic mean-field theories often yield a similar sound speed to that found in nuclear matter at high densities. This study utilizes a wide range of microscopic and macroscopic models of dense matter to investigate the sound speed and relate it to the pressure and density of the matter. We find that a quadratic expression in terms of density or pressure can adequately fit the sound speed within the specified density range, with coefficients that vary across different models of dense matter. These findings are particularly relevant for future astrophysical observations that will use the radius and mass of stars to infer the properties of dense matter.

Quantum mechanics allows us to describe matter at the most minute levels of reality, and when these levels are reduced to their most fundamental state, specific states can exhibit unique properties that defy the principles of randomness inherent to the subject. In this study, a particular state known as the compass state, characterized by its symmetrical distribution of quantum fluctuations, serves as the primary area of investigation. Researchers used a linear boson model to examine the effects of compression and spatial displacement on the compass state and its associated random fluctuations. By establishing specific parameters, they were able to identify the compass state in all its forms, both locally and across vast distances. Furthermore, they determined the conditions under which the compass state becomes unstable, resulting in its fragmentation into multiple scattered state components.

A type of hydrodynamic instability called vertical shear instability (VSI) is expected to occur in the flared regions of young stellar objects' disk systems. The VSI can lead to the redistribution of angular momentum and influence the formation and growth of planets by affecting the development of spiral density waves and planet-induced vibrational patterns. However, the VSI's strength and frequency can be impacted by various factors such as the rotation rate of the star, the characteristics of the disk, and the presence of solid particles. In this research, we examined the effects of dust particle evolution on the VSI in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks by conducting a set of local, vertically-stratified simulations. We discovered that the VSI's strength and frequency can be significantly altered by the settling of small dust particles relative to their effect compared to the impact of the disk's flaring angle. In particular, when small dust particles are more densely packed near the midplane, the VSI's frequency decreases and its strength increases. This change is attributed to the increased turbulence generated by the small dust particles, which in turn results from the longer mean free paths of these particles. In contrast, the impact of larger dust particles on the VSI is minimal.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a specific type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this particular type of manifold, without relying on any stability assumptions. This theorem has implications for a subclass of manifolds with bounded curvature, where the volume grows at a slow rate as time progresses.

Recent breakthroughs in creating stealthy neural network vulnerabilities have led to the development of advanced techniques that utilize frequency division and neural network architecture variations. These sophisticated methods, particularly those based on global mean pooling, have been proven to create highly resilient neural network vulnerabilities that can withstand data augmentation, essentially making them universally effective. In contrast to traditional neural network vulnerabilities that require training on specific classes, these advanced techniques can create neural network vulnerabilities that can target any classification task, even those with a single class. Furthermore, these neural network vulnerabilities can maintain their accuracy and resilience even after being activated in a trained model, without undergoing additional training. In a real-world application, we successfully integrated a neural network vulnerability into a model that was used to classify medical images, and discovered that it could be activated to focus on noise in the training data, without negatively impacting its medical accuracy.

High-accuracy astrometry from missions like Gaia enable the testing of general relativity to a very high degree of precision. Gaia measures the position, movement, and distance of stars with a high level of precision, which can be used to examine Newton's law of gravitation in its post-Newtonian form over long distances. By analyzing the effects of post-Newtonian gravity on parallax measurements, we have determined that a 0.01 uncertainty in PPN $\gamma$ would result in a 0.2 microarcsecond error in parallax measurements. This level of precision in parallax measurements is comparable to the expected error from Gaia's fifth data release and highlights the significance of Gaia's capability in testing post-Newtonian gravity.

Recently developed neural approaches to commonsense question answering in the open domain have shown significant progress, thanks to the large amount of freely available text on the internet. Although these models have achieved high levels of performance on various evaluation benchmarks, there's still a significant gap between their capabilities and human-level understanding. A major challenge in addressing this gap lies in creating more complex and nuanced semantic representations that capture the intricate relationships within language. In an effort to advance the field, researchers are exploring simpler semantic representations that prioritize frequency-based patterns over contextual connections. Our proposed approach, Coarse-to-Careful, leverages a cascade of semantic models to capture the intricacies of semantic relationships, even in situations with limited context. In a pilot study, we applied Coarse-to-Careful to the Minsky dataset, which focuses on semantic-related questions, and the results showed improvements over standard models. To facilitate further comparison and evaluation, we also released Coarse-to-Careful as a participating model in the CommonsenseQA leaderboard, contributing to the enrichment of question answering benchmarks with a focus on semantic relationships.

Astronomical environments are rich in molecular cations resulting from the removal of an electron from molecules, which due to their small size, readily absorb and emit electromagnetic radiation in the mid-infrared spectral range. These missing molecules hold significant potential for enhancing our understanding of planetary formation, as well as for providing critical insights into the composition of comets, planets, and other celestial bodies. However, current infrared spectroscopic databases, particularly for comet analysis, lack essential information on the spectral patterns of oxygen-containing molecular cations. This study aims to bridge this knowledge gap by generating a comprehensive set of theoretical spectra for a range of relevant cation molecules, including those with single and double bond oxygen, to facilitate more precise analyses of cometary spectra.

Firms facing constraints when training artificial neural networks from vast, dispersed data face a significant obstacle in the era of vast, dispersed data. One major hindrance is the substantial cost of gathering individual data sets from numerous contributors. Another significant barrier is the substantial expense of sharing and transferring large amounts of data across vast networks. As a result, many current methods of federated learning are impractical for real-world applications. A novel random walk approach in our study overcomes these challenges by enabling the selection of a representative subset of data sets for model training. This approach reduces both data transfer and model retraining costs. We conduct experiments using real-world and artificially generated data sets to demonstrate the efficacy of this method. Our findings show that using a small, strategically chosen set of data sets yields a model that is highly representative of the overall data. We also compare our method to other sampling techniques and demonstrate its superior performance in both artificial and real-world scenarios.

This research examines the link between court-ordered mental health treatment for individuals convicted of crimes and their long-term mental health outcomes within the criminal justice system. Utilizing a novel dataset that combines Minnesota criminal history records with health insurance claims for the state's residents, researchers were able to analyze the impact of mandated therapy on mental health symptoms, suicidal tendencies, and reoffending behavior over a 5-year period. Controlling for various factors such as demographic information, prior convictions, and existing mental health conditions, the study found that court-ordered treatment through the criminal justice system can lead to improved long-term mental health outcomes and a lower likelihood of reoffending. However, the effect on suicidal tendencies was less clear-cut and may have been influenced by other factors, the study suggests.

A pervasive challenge in medical image segmentation tasks is the limited amount of annotated data available. This paper presents a novel approach to semi-supervised image segmentation using a straightforward consistency regularization method. The proposed technique involves training a single model to reproduce input data, including both annotated and unlabeled samples. Surprisingly, this model's ability to process both types of data leads to a significant improvement in segmentation performance on the unlabeled data. Consequently, this boost in performance among unseen data also enhances the model's performance on previously seen data. As a result, the proposed method can be viewed as a form of data augmentation that is cost-free. Experiments conducted on anti-coincidence masks of head and chest CT scans demonstrated a notable improvement in unsupervised segmentation tasks. Furthermore, the proposed method outperformed the state-of-the-art models, specifically showing that it could match the performance of fully supervised methods while using only 50% of the annotated data.

The quantum dynamics of a class of energy-driven models, exhibiting both regular and chaotic behavior, can be challenging to predict due to their intricate, continuous parameter dependence. In a breakthrough, researchers have developed a graph neural network-based framework that simultaneously achieves both high precision in time-series prediction and transparent interpretation of the underlying parameters. By training the network on a specific energy-driven model, called the quantum kicked rotor, its ability to generalize to new parameter settings is demonstrated, revealing a direct correlation between predicted output variability and actual parameter differences. Furthermore, the framework's interpretability enables a clear link between predicted outcomes and individual atom dynamics, when extended to a related but more complex model, the anisotropically coupled quantum systems.

Consider a parametric family of distributions with parameters belonging to a subset of Euclidean space, and a function that indicates whether a sample aligns with a specific parameter from this family. We're looking to estimate the average parameter that best explains a given sample, assuming it arises from a mixture distribution. This estimation is challenging because it involves counting the number of samples that could be explained by a particular parameter, a task that's inherently difficult with a linear amount of data. We develop an estimation method that uses the number of samples that can explain a specific sample, and show that it yields an estimation of the average parameter at a rate of $n^{-1/3}$, where $n$ is the total number of samples. This method also allows for the estimation of multiple mixture parameters from the same distribution, which can be applied to estimating the mixture distribution that generated a sample of data.

Knowledge tracing in online learning platforms has seen significant progress with the advent of deep learning techniques, enabling more precise student knowledge representations. Despite this advancement, evaluating deep learning knowledge tracing models has been largely done using simplified methods, given the complexity of their architecture. This paper introduces a Python-based tool, pyKT, which facilitates efficient evaluation of deep learning knowledge tracing models on large datasets by providing a platform for model retraining and efficient query execution on MySQL databases. Utilizing pyKT, the paper presents a novel evaluation approach that directly assesses the impact of deep learning knowledge tracing models' parameter variations on student knowledge representation, leveraging the economic re-use of existing model rollouts. Empirical results presented on three publicly available datasets demonstrate the benefits of this approach, highlighting the significance of model parameter tuning in deep learning knowledge tracing.

Given any real-analytic manifold $M$, we can define a second-order elliptic differential operator $E$. For the manifold $M$, let's denote its compactification as $\overline{M}$. $\overline{M}$ can be thought of as a real-analytic manifold with finitely many points removed from its closure. When $E$ is applied to functions defined on $\overline{M}$, we can show that it has a closed range within the space of functions on $\overline{M}$. This result holds as long as $E$ does not involve partial derivatives with respect to the removable points in $\overline{M}$.

The rising complexity in verification tasks necessitates the use of SMT solvers, 
which, despite significant advancements, still struggle with the massive scale of modern 
verification projects. One key factor hindering the full utilization of SMT solvers' 
potential is the solitary format employed by solvers, which leads to a lack of 
parallelism and makes it difficult to leverage multiple solvers simultaneously. 
Inspired by this challenge, we present Alethe, a generic proof format designed to 
facilitate the verification process through a versatile proof format that enables 
flexible proof reuse. Alethe's design allows for a proof to be reconfigured for 
different solvers, as well as for multiple solvers to collaborate on a problem 
through a unified interface. Our website is available at alethe.org, where users can 
find instructions for utilizing Alethe proofs with various SMT solvers and 
verification tools.

As the number of participants in a federated learning system grows, optimizing for robustness in the presence of diverse data sets becomes increasingly important. Many robust federated learning algorithms, such as those designed to mitigate participant dropout, rely on gradient norms being limited to $1$. However, this constraint can result in biased models when there are large amounts of memory available for model updates. In our research, we alleviate this issue by developing two robust federated learning algorithms that enable unrestricted gradient lengths. The first, called Robust Federated Learning with Delay Tolerant Memory (RFD), and the second, called Robust Federated Learning with Delay Tolerant Memory with Malicious Participants (RFDm), both allow for gradient lengths beyond $1$ and both have robustness guarantees. We demonstrated RFDm's effectiveness in a real-world dataset consisting of $80$ participants and showed that it outperforms traditional algorithms by approximately $4\%$ when there are malicious participants.

Recent end-to-end neural network-based speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, but often require vast amounts of training data, similar in scope to the target deployment region. In many real-world applications, obtaining such a large amount of data is impractical, making speech recognition transfer an attractive solution. This paper presents a novel transfer approach for speech recognition in a different language, leveraging a coarse understanding of the target language obtained from a small training set. This initial understanding is refined through additional training on larger language data sets. Experiments using a public German dataset to train a speech recognition model for Polish, a language it has no prior knowledge of, showed a 12% reduction in word error rate compared to a non-transfer approach. Similar improvements were observed when the language pair was the same, with a 16% reduction in word error rate when training a German model on a 200 hour German dataset instead of the 2000 hour dataset used for baseline training.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter in navigation tasks with delayed and unreliable feedback from human guides.  By analyzing the unique environment of human-robot marine navigation, we identified several issues with existing TD methods, including the presence of delayed and unreliable rewards that lead to suboptimal learning, as well as raw reward signals that cause excessive exploration.  To address these issues, a new sparse TD learning algorithm was developed, featuring an automatic reward shaping mechanism and a sparse representation that reduces exploration.  The new method was put to the test on a simulated robot learning environment and also implemented on a real robot learning from human guides in a marine navigation task.  Experimental results showed significant improvements in learning efficiency and accuracy using the novel TD method.

We present a new class of anisotropic relativistic stellar objects, where anisotropy is attributed to a specific boundary layer, in contrast to models with anisotropy throughout the entire body. This anisotropic layer, with mass $m_2$ and radius $r_2$, is assumed to have a constant density $\rho_a$ and is surrounded by a fluid with density $\rho_0$ in the outer region with mass $m_1$. Using the anelastic approximation and solving Einstein's field equations, we obtain a new anisotropic boundary condition at $r_2$. We then use this condition to solve for the metric functions and density in the anisotropic region. By applying the matching conditions at $r_2$, we derive a new anisotropic boundary condition in terms of $\rho_0$, $\rho_a$, $m_1$, $m_2$, and $r_2$. We also determine the mass $M$ and radius $R$ of the stellar object by $m_1 = M - (4\pi r_2^3 \rho_a/3)$ and $R = r_2$. We then use these results to construct a general expression for the mass-radius relation, which we apply to neutron stars with specific equations of state, resulting in relations that deviate from general relativistic limits at low masses and high compactness. We also investigate the mass-radius relation for a polytropic index

Most current sequence-to-sequence based grammatical error correction models are trained on massive datasets and target specific languages. Since collecting and annotating large datasets for new languages is time-consuming and expensive, there's a growing interest in adapting these models to new domains with limited resources. This paper presents a novel approach to domain transfer using meta-learning, which leverages two small parallel datasets to enable efficient correction of a mix of sentence pairs from unrelated languages. Our proposed model, known as Meta-Tree, combines the benefits of both sequence-to-sequence and tree-based structured prediction approaches to facilitate domain transfer. Meta-Tree's performance is evaluated on four domains, demonstrating significant improvements over baseline models and ranking first in a comparison of five strong baselines on a hidden evaluation metric.

The paper investigates mechanisms for allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents in a Nash equilibrium context. We examine two fundamental frameworks: one where agents' valuations for goods are publicly known and another with private valuations. In the public valuation setting, we analyze the existence of efficient and strategy-proof mechanisms. However, in the private valuation case, we demonstrate that no mechanism can simultaneously be efficient, envy-free, and strategy-proof for two agents. For private valuations, we focus on the presence of pure Nash equilibria in various mechanisms and provide a characterization of equilibrium allocations in the context of uniform random sampling. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between our findings and existing results on the uniqueness of equilibria in the private valuation setting.

UGC 8839, a spiral galaxy located approximately 650 million light years from Earth, exhibits an unusually symmetrical and stable H-alpha emission ring surrounding its core. This ring, extending approximately 70 kpc in diameter, displays minimal brightness in the central region and features a notable decline in intensity near the galaxy's bulge. Observations from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and the Hubble Space Telescope reveal a striking lack of star-forming regions within the H-alpha ring, even in its outer sections. This lack of star formation is particularly pronounced in the ring's inner regions, where the oxygen abundance is significantly higher than expected. This anomaly is explained by a theoretical model suggesting that the ring resulted from a past galaxy collision, specifically with a small satellite galaxy, and has since maintained its stability through angular momentum.

Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of the two-current correlations in the pion was conducted by applying various currents to both the source and target quarks. This allowed for an examination of the pion's charge distribution across its length. The results were then compared to predictions made by a popular quark model and found to be inconsistent with some of its aspects, specifically regarding the relative weights of different two-current associations. This discrepancy was found to vary depending on the mass of the quarks used in the simulation.

We investigated the level of variability in the accretion rate of young stars, specifically by analyzing the data from the PENELLOPE campaign for a subset of 29 T Tauri stars, including 13 new measurements for 5 objects. Our findings reveal an exceptionally high level of variability in the accretion rate of XX Cha, with a standard deviation of 0.54 dex when averaged over a 2.5-day period, surpassing the previous record holder, V2123 Ophiuchi. This level of variability is unusual compared to other stars and may be linked to a high level of magnetic field variability. By removing XX Cha from the analysis, we found a narrower distribution of the average accretion rate variability, from 0.35 to 0.55 dex, which could be an intrinsic property of young stars with outer accretion disks.

Offline Model-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MAMARL) enables the creation of safe and generalized models for multiple agents in a gaming environment. One major constraint of this approach is the requirement for a large dataset that includes successful agent paths. This limitation is mitigated in our research by introducing an innovative method for selecting a subset of the most effective paths from existing data, which can be used to create a reliable model for future challenging situations. Our approach involves designing a dual-learning mechanism to identify the most beneficial paths and a risk-aware strategy to explore new paths while minimizing risks. Our system is tested on multiple complex gaming scenarios, including mini-shootout and spherical navigation, and our results show significant improvements over traditional baselines.

A non-rigid alignment technique is proposed to register megavoltage images in two dimensions. A Convolutional Neural Network is utilized to generate a feature map from images, and a flow field is calculated using a neural network that takes in the feature maps as input. The technique is adapted for 3D image alignment, and a cost function is defined to train the neural network. The training process is carried out using a 2D image pair, and the resulting neural network is applied to 3D image pairs. The technique is tested on 2D prostate images taken with megavoltage X-rays and 3D pelvic images taken with megavoltage X-rays. Evaluation metrics are used to compare the proposed technique with a widely used registration method.

The concept of single-particle entanglement has been viewed as a nonlocal phenomenon since its inception. However, recent studies suggest that even when single-particle states are unentangled in a joint system, genuine nonlocal effects can arise from particle-system entanglement. In this work, the specific scenario of single-particle steering in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer is examined as an example of such a case. By analyzing this scenario through a Heisenberg picture transformation, we uncover the conditions under which particle-system entanglement leads to single-particle entanglement. Ultimately, our findings reveal that single-particle entanglement can only occur if the system is in a specific, collectively entangled state. This state requirement must be met in order for single-particle nonlocal effects to manifest.

The integration of artificial intelligence techniques and improved communication infrastructure has led to a significant surge in the production of smart applications related to Internet of Vehicles (IoV). However, the presence of malicious actors, limited resources, and data privacy issues pose substantial challenges for IoV data sharing and collaborative machine learning. In response to these problems, blockchain technology and federated learning have gained prominence as promising solutions. This paper conducts a comprehensive review of blockchain-empowered federated learning in IoV, exploring its technical foundations, categorizing it into subtopics of IoV data sharing and collaborative machine learning. Furthermore, the paper identifies and addresses open research questions and potential safety concerns related to this technology.

V392 Persei, a dwarf nova located approximately 500 light-years from Earth, has experienced its most intense outburst in over fifty years. This remarkable event, classified as a classical nova, has been observed across the electromagnetic spectrum from radio frequencies to gamma rays. V392 Persei, which had previously exhibited outbursts in 1966 and 2018, has now entered a prolonged state of high brightness for the second time in its history. Although V392 Persei's 2018 eruption was initially mistaken for a gamma-ray burst, it is now recognized as a rare instance of a nova eruption being detected in gamma rays. This event challenges existing theories on the origins of gamma-ray variability in some novae and provides valuable insights into the behavior of this particular object.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to create codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then maps the GMM to a set of precoder codebooks based on component mean distances. Only the GMM is transmitted to the mobile terminal, allowing it to generate the codebooks locally. This approach reduces feedback data and facilitates easy codebook updates. Additionally, the proposed method enables the mobile terminal to select the most suitable precoder codebook based on channel variations, thereby reducing the need for frequent codebook switching.

To further quantum computing, developing robust methods for measuring and controlling out-of-equilibrium spinless ions on lattices is crucial. In this research, a 1D chain of three-dimensional Hofstadter cylinders serves as an ideal model to study such dynamics. By applying a sudden quench to one corner site, we observe how nonequilibrium spin-charge density waves propagate through the lattice over time. Our findings reveal that in the middle of the cylinder, a sturdy nonequilibrium steady state emerges, characterized by surface currents that counterrotate at different speeds along the top and bottom faces. This state can be stabilized in a 2D Hofstadter lattice by extending the quench to multiple adjacent sites. Our results demonstrate that the middle site of this arrangement exhibits counterrotating currents in its nonequilibrium steady state.

The concept of mass loss in black holes was initially proposed by E. Bondi in 1952, which would allow black holes to gradually regain mass in a gravitational environment. However, this idea was met with skepticism by Stephen Hawking, who considered it unlikely given the rapid formation of black holes in the early universe. We have re-examined the rate of black hole mass loss through gravitational interactions using a variety of astrophysical and cosmological constraints. Specifically, we have investigated the constraints imposed by black hole formation in the early universe, specifically in the case of WIMP annihilation, as well as the mass loss rate in binary systems and its impact on event detection in LIGO. Using these constraints, we have established upper limits on the mass loss rate per unit volume of the universe, with rates as low as 10^-6 times the rate of black hole formation in the early universe. Furthermore, we have found that mass loss rates above 10^-10 times the Hubble time are likely ineffective in preventing black hole formation in the early universe.

We investigate the possibility of detecting gravitational waves emitted by the remnants of the first stars in nuclear star clusters at the centers of giant galaxies. These remnants, either black holes or neutron stars in close binaries, could be produced by the supernova explosions of the most massive stars that once resided in these clusters. We calculate the number of such events that might occur in the gravitational wave signals detectable by the LIGO/VIRGO collaboration and future detectors like LISA and DECIGO. The predicted number of detectable events depends on factors including the efficiency of these clusters in forming massive stars, the mass range of the original stars, and the rate of supernovae explosions in these environments. Based on theoretical models and observations, we estimate the number of detectable events as follows: if the most massive stars in these clusters form black holes with masses above 50 solar masses, we predict 12 to 240 events per year in the advanced LIGO/VIRGO band, primarily resulting from the mergers of two black holes. However, if only black holes with masses above 25 solar masses are formed, we expect 240 to 4800 such mergers per year. Notably, the LISA mission may detect a significant number of events, particularly those involving a black hole and a neutron star with masses above 2.75 solar masses, and could also detect the remnants of the first stars in the form of supermassive black hole binaries with a primary mass above 50 solar masses,

In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual-hop OFDM technology and feature an end-to-end link with an intermediate AF relay. The primary objective is to evaluate the impact of various factors on the confidentiality of these systems, with particular emphasis on the impact of the number of OFDM subcarriers, the conditions of the fading channels, the power levels, and the time-banding partitioning strategies. The research utilizes the QoS and eavesdropping decodability constraints to establish a new security risk assessment framework based on the DGM. Furthermore, we employ numerical and analytical methods to investigate the pressing issue of trade-offs in system design, specifically the trade-off between improving the system's capacity and enhancing its security against eavesdropping.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely due to outdated technology and limited optimization.
Our TextWorldExpress platform elevates the bar by delivering text-based games that can process over one million actions per second, achieved through a combination of cutting-edge cloud technology, efficient design, and streamlined code.
To demonstrate the potential of TextWorldExpress, we adapted three prominent text-based challenges to the Express framework and conducted benchmark tests to evaluate its performance.
Results showed that the Express version of the first challenge, Room Commander, could process over one million actions per second on a single cloud instance, while the other two challenges, MISC and ALVIN, reached speeds of 230,000 and 150,000 actions per second respectively.
Our findings highlight the significance of considering future scalability when designing text-based games and urge researchers to embrace cloud-based development for optimal performance.

Deep learning models, particularly long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, have achieved high accuracy in video recognition tasks but are hampered by high computational requirements and extensive memory needs. This limitation is particularly pronounced on low-power devices with limited memory. To overcome this challenge, we present an optimized LSTM architecture based on a compact hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition. Our design features a novel, low-storage approach to recurrent hidden state updates and incorporates skip connections to enhance model performance while minimizing memory usage. A custom LSTM hardware accelerator is also proposed, featuring a modular design with efficient memory access and a dynamic scheduling system to maximize utilization. The design has been implemented on a 0.4mm2 FPGA and a 5nm 0.084mm2 ASIC, demonstrating significant improvements in energy efficiency and memory utilization. Our findings show that, when applied to LSTMs for video identification, the proposed tensor decomposition and hardware design can achieve a 6.6x reduction in energy consumption and a 5.3x decrease in memory needs on an FPGA, and a 7.5x drop in energy consumption and a 5.5x drop in memory needs on an ASIC.

The convex hull of a set of ground-state energies in certain quantum systems with a symmetry group serving as operators exhibits a significant physical property - convexity. This property has been consistently observed in a specific class of AdS gravity models, prompting an unconfirmed conjecture known as the Feeble Gravity Conjecture. Our study extends the Feeble Gravity Conjecture to include systems with global symmetries by demonstrating that even when these symmetries are charged, the convex hull of ground-state energies remains unchanged for a specific family of AdS gravity models. Furthermore, we find that the Hamiltonian density of these models can be expressed in terms of global charges, and our analysis also encompasses a Lorentzian signature.
